Case facts and general practice, stage by stage. The bench stage isn’t in the article, so there is only general practice.
In this case: a 2018 DAF 106; the engine control module wouldn’t communicate with the scan tool and the engine wouldn’t start.

Usual practice: record the complaint in the customer’s words, the VIN, the module and software numbers and what has already been done to the vehicle; photograph the housing, connector and mounting before removal. Give the time and price after diagnosis. What to record for yourself is in the lesson “Testing after repair and handing over to the customer.”
Vehicle first, then the module

In this case: the article states it plainly — no communication with a module doesn’t always mean a faulty processor: power, ground and wiring problems look the same, and the cause has to be found by testing.

Usual practice: the module’s fuses and relays, the battery isolator switch, +30, +15 and grounds at the connector under load, the CAN bus, a look at the connector — the order is in the lesson “A module that won’t communicate,” and the 24 V specifics in “Truck and heavy equipment modules.” The module comes off only once the vehicle checks out.
On the bench
In this case: the article doesn’t describe any bench measurements — it only says the module was taken apart.

Usual practice: connect the module to a current-limited power supply using a verified diagram — 24 V for the DAF — and check the current, 5 V, the crystal and the transceiver, as in the lessons “Connecting a module on the bench” and “A module that won’t communicate.”
Usual practice: before heating the processor, save a full memory backup if it can be read — see the lesson “Module memory and backups.”
The board and the repair

In this case: the fault was lost contact in the solder joints under the processor. The processor is in a BGA package: its pins connect to the board through solder balls. When those joints are damaged the module can stop working and communicating, and the processor itself doesn’t have to shift — cracks and lost contact in the solder are enough. The module sits on anti-vibration mounts, which lose their elasticity over time and damp vibration less well. Another blog article, on the DAF 105 and 106, names vibration and worn mounts as one of the most common reasons these modules fail.

In this case: the module was taken apart, the processor removed from the board and reballed — its ball contacts restored — then put back and soldered; the module was reassembled and fitted to the truck.

Usual practice: BGA work needs proper equipment and experience, as the lesson “Soldering and replacing components” says: bottom preheating of the board, a stencil and balls of the right size, flux, then cleaning and inspection under magnification; neighboring parts are shielded from heat.

Never leave a BGA station or hot-air tool unattended, and work under fume extraction: flux fumes are harmful. Don’t heat the processor until you’ve saved a memory backup, if it can be read, and don’t overheat the board — the settings are chosen for the specific board.

When I repair a module that has suffered from vibration, I look not only at the board but at the mounting too. If the anti-vibration mounts have hardened or are damaged, they damp vibration poorly, and the repaired module will take the same punishment. So I always take the mounts into account.
Testing and handover
In this case: the ECU communicated with the scan tool again, the engine started, and the module was saved without a full replacement.
Usual practice on the bench: current, communication and part numbers, memory compared with the backup, an extended run, light tapping and gentle heating — a must after any solder repair.
Usual practice in the vehicle: codes in all modules before and after a drive, starting, live data, a drive in the conditions where the fault appeared; hardened mounting bushings are replaced.

Usual practice: a report for the customer — the complaint, what was found (lost contact in the solder under the processor), what was done (reballing), the outside cause (vibration, the state of the mounts), photos of the board, the warranty and its terms. More in the lesson “Testing after repair and handing over to the customer.”

Not just the engine: ABS, BCM, automatic transmission, instrument cluster — hardware repair

How the ABS module, body control module, automatic transmission module and instrument cluster are built and what most often fails in them, what gets repaired on the board, what to do after the repair, and which jobs we don’t take on.

The engine module isn’t the only “computer” in a car. The ABS module, the body control module (BCM), the automatic transmission module and the instrument cluster are built the same way: power supply and regulator, processor, inputs, output stages, bus transceivers — as in the lesson “What’s inside an ECU”. But each has its own operating conditions, its own typical failures and its own limits: what can be repaired on the board and what can’t.

First make sure the module really is at fault. The blog has a write-up on a 2019 Volkswagen Polo: the ABS light was on, the turn signals, hazard lights and brake lights didn’t work, and the ABS module wouldn’t communicate — code U012100 was stored in several modules at once. The fuses were checked with a test light, then the power at the ABS module: one of the two power feeds had no voltage. When power was applied to that circuit as a diagnostic check, the module came online. So there’s no need to remove the module — the next step is checking the wiring against the diagram.
Check the fuses first. A fuse that looks intact proves nothing yet, so I check it with a test light: that shows whether the circuit has voltage under a small load.

ABS and ESP

An ABS unit usually has two parts: a hydraulic unit with valves and a pump, and an electronic module. The valve coils sit in the module and slide over the valve stems, and the pump motor is connected to the module by power terminals.

Typical hardware failures: cracked solder joints and corrosion on the coil and pump motor terminals, an open coil winding, a burnt valve or pump motor driver, and the power feed and connector — water and road salt get there.

Signs: codes for the valves, the pump, supply voltage or an internal module fault. Wheel speed sensor codes mean the sensor, connector and wiring first, as in the lesson “Other systems and scan tool service functions”.

An example from the blog: on a Toyota Prado 150, after suspension repairs, the ABS light came on now and then with code C1414 — the front left wheel speed sensor circuit. The sensor and connector were checked, the sensor was removed and cleaned of dirt, and the owner was advised to come back for diagnostics if the code returned. The ABS module itself wasn’t touched.

On many units the electronic module comes off the hydraulic unit without opening the brake system. If the brake system was opened, bleed it following the manufacturer’s procedure, often with a scan tool.

The valve coils are in the electronic module; the weak spots are the solder joints on their pins and on the pump motor pins.

ABS and ESP are safety systems. On the board, restore only the factory circuit: the same part or a direct equivalent per the datasheet. A homemade transistor replacement for a channel, as in the lesson “A burnt-out driver: building a replacement from transistors”, is not done here. After the repair: codes in all modules, wheel speeds in live data, bleeding if the brakes were opened, and a braking check at low speed in a safe area. The car goes back with a firm pedal and no ABS codes.
The body control module switches the lights, turn signals, brake lights, locks, wipers and heaters — through relays on the board and power transistors. It’s often combined with the fuse box.

Water is the main enemy: through a leaking glass seal, a clogged drain, the sunroof or the A/C. That brings corrosion, eaten-away traces and shorts, as in the lesson “Moisture, corrosion and vibration”. Until the leak is found, the board repair isn’t finished.

Relays on the board: burnt or welded contacts. Power transistors: they burn out after a short in the turn signal, brake light or parking light wiring. A new transistor goes in only after the short is found, otherwise it will burn out the same way, as in the lesson “Output stages: why they burn out and how to test them”.

The body control module often stores immobilizer and key data and the equipment coding. Before the repair, make a memory backup, as in the lesson “Module memory and backups”. We don’t touch immobilizer and key data: if pairing is needed after the repair, it’s done at a dealer or by the manufacturer’s procedure, and only with the vehicle documents.
Automatic transmission module
A transmission module can be separate — in the cabin or under the hood — or built into the gearbox together with the valve body. A built-in one takes the heat of the oil and the vibration.

Hardware failures: cracked solder joints, the power supply and regulator, solenoid outputs, the connector and ribbon cables, water in a separate module. Clutch packs, the valve body and the mechanicals are for a transmission specialist.

Before opening it up: codes, live data and a check of what the transmission receives — the brake signal, selector position, power. The blog has a Range Rover Evoque whose rotary gear selector didn’t work: the cause turned out to be the transport mode lock, and no module repair was needed.
After repairing or replacing the module: reset the adaptations and run the transmission relearn by the manufacturer’s procedure, as in the lesson “Adaptations and resets”.
The needles are driven by stepper motors. A needle that sticks, jumps or doesn’t return to zero means a worn stepper motor or a cracked solder joint on its pins.
Part of the dial is dark — a backlight LED, its resistor or its transistor. The cluster goes dark over bumps — cracked solder at the connector pins or a power problem.
As with other modules, the fuse, connectors, ground and power come first, then the board — the blog article “Instrument cluster not working” covers this.

Our cluster repair is hardware only: motors, backlight, soldering, power, display. We don’t read, write or transfer the memory that holds the mileage. The odometer is photographed at intake and at handover — the readings must match.

The line is simple: we take hardware repairs and restore the factory circuit. We don’t take airbag (SRS) modules after a crash: after deployment the module stores crash data, and it’s replaced together with the deployed parts by the manufacturer’s procedure, as in the lesson “Other systems and scan tool service functions”. We also don’t take work on the mileage memory, immobilizer and key data, or modified software — as in the lesson “Module memory and backups”.

Official reprogramming: J2534, dealer portals, secure gateways

When a module software update counts as a repair, how it’s written officially — through a J2534 adapter and the manufacturer’s portal or dealer equipment — how to hold the voltage while programming, what to do if programming is interrupted, how to work with a secure gateway, and what we don’t do.

Sometimes a fault is fixed not with a soldering iron or a new part but with a new version of the module software. The manufacturer finds a bug in the software — say, harsh transmission shifts or a false code — and releases an update along with a service bulletin. What each type of equipment can do was covered in the lesson “Scan tools and adapters: what to choose and how to connect”. Here: how to write an update officially without damaging the module.
When an update is a repair
There’s a manufacturer service bulletin or recall that matches the customer’s complaint and applies to this VIN. The software number in the module is older than the one in the bulletin.
The module was replaced with a new one: it often arrives with no software or a base version, and the software is written by the manufacturer’s procedure.
Don’t update “just in case”. New software with no complaint and no bulletin fixes nothing, and afterward adaptations may be needed.
Software won’t fix a broken wire, a poor ground or a faulty sensor. Normal diagnostics come first: codes, live data, measurements, as in the lesson “The scan tool diagnostic procedure”.
The official route: J2534 and the manufacturer’s portal

J2534 is an SAE recommended practice for a “pass-through” adapter, PassThru. It only connects the computer to the car; the software, files and access rights come from the manufacturer — through its service portal on a subscription (for a day, several days or a year) or through dealer equipment. The manufacturer’s software also checks the right to program: in a 2020 Toyota bulletin, the module requires a digital signature during the update, which the software gets from the manufacturer’s portal. In Kazakhstan, portal access depends on the make — check with the official distributor. Gray-market imports may have no manufacturer support: the blog has an article on this using the Zeekr 001 as an example.

The manufacturer supplies the software and files, the J2534 adapter just passes them to the module, and the power supply holds the voltage.
Power and communication while programming

Connect a power supply that holds a steady voltage under load — not an ordinary battery charger and not a jump from another car. The voltage follows the manufacturer’s requirements: in the same Toyota bulletin, 13.5 V from the power supply and no lower than 11.8 V during programming; other makes have their own figures.
Switch off everything you don’t need: headlights, climate control, heaters, the radio. Doors, hood and key position as the procedure requires.
Laptop on its charger, sleep mode and automatic updates off, a stable internet connection. The adapter cable isn’t pulled tight and can’t get underfoot.

While programming, don’t switch off the ignition, unplug the adapter or start other programs. Lights on the dash may flash: other modules briefly lose contact with the one being programmed — that’s no reason to stop.

A voltage drop or a dropout mid-write can leave the module without working software, and it will stop communicating. The blog article “Why Kia and Hyundai ECUs fail” lists attempts to “flash it on the spot” and cheap equipment among the causes.

Without a power supply the voltage sags under load and programming can abort; with a power supply it stays steady.
If programming is interrupted
Don’t unplug anything in a hurry: check the power, the adapter connection and the internet.
Repeat the programming with the same manufacturer software, following its prompts: many programs can retry the write or recover the module.
If that doesn’t work, contact the manufacturer’s support or a dealer.
Don’t write some “random” file from the internet: it may be for a different module version and carry another car’s data, as in the lesson “Module memory and backups” in the ECU Repair course.
Secure gateway

Many newer cars have a secure gateway, SGW, between the diagnostic connector and the modules — the same gateway as in the lesson “No communication: the scan tool can’t see the modules”, only protected. Without authorization a scan tool reads codes and live data, while clearing codes, active tests and, depending on the make, coding and programming are locked. On some Jeep, Chrysler, Dodge and Fiat vehicles from about the 2017–2018 model years, access is opened by registering the shop and the scan tool with AutoAuth. On Volkswagen and Audi the similar protection is called SFD: it’s unlocked through a manufacturer account or purchased access. Some Nissan and Mercedes-Benz models also require authorization.

Without authorization the gateway lets only reading through; after official registration the service functions open up.

What we don’t do: modified software — chip tuning and “emissions-off” software that disables EGR, the DPF, AdBlue/SCR or the catalytic converter; mileage changes; disabling the immobilizer, including “via a flash”; bypassing a secure gateway and working through someone else’s account. We write only the manufacturer’s official software for this VIN, or our own verified file for the same module from a backup. Such changes break the law, and whoever made them is responsible — as in the lesson “Adaptations and resets”.
It’s better to get a Launch scan tool — it’s proven equipment. Cheap ELM327 adapters sometimes “knock out” the car, and in the middle of programming such a dropout can cost you the module.

A secure gateway is opened only by official registration; modified software, mileage, immobilizers and gateway bypasses — we don’t do.

ADAS after repairs: what the scan tool shows and when calibration is needed

Which sensors help the driver — the camera, radars, surround-view cameras and parking sensors — what codes the scan tool shows for them, which jobs call for calibration by the manufacturer’s procedure, how static calibration differs from dynamic, and why it’s never done “by eye”.

ADAS means driver assistance systems: automatic emergency braking, adaptive cruise control, lane keeping, blind-spot monitoring, surround-view cameras. They’ve long been more than a luxury-car feature: Jetour, Chery, Haval, Changan and Geely were all in the top ten for new-car sales in Kazakhstan in January–October 2025, and these systems now come on mass-market models too. An auto electrician’s job is to recognize when calibration is needed, check what’s within reach — power, connectors, communication — and send the car for calibration by the manufacturer’s procedure, not set sensors “by eye”.
Where the sensors are
The front camera is on the windshield behind the mirror: lane markings, signs, vehicles and pedestrians.
The front radar is behind the badge, the grille or in the bumper: the distance and speed of the car ahead for cruise control and braking.
Corner radars are in the rear and sometimes the front bumper: blind spots and backing out.
Surround-view cameras are in the mirrors, grille and liftgate; ultrasonic parking sensors are in the bumpers.
The systems also need data from other modules: wheel speeds from ABS, steering angle, turn signal status. So an ADAS code can be the result of a fault in a completely different system.

The camera looks through the windshield and the radars through the bumper and badge: any repair near them can knock their angle out.
What the scan tool shows
Calibration codes: “camera not calibrated”, “radar not aligned”, “alignment out of range”. On some cars, live data shows the calibration status and the sensor’s mounting angles.
Temporary blocking: “radar blocked”, “camera view restricted”. Causes: snow, ice, dirt, a sticker, a fogged windshield, bright sun. Clean the sensor and check on a drive: no calibration needed here.

Power and communication: lost communication with the camera or radar, low voltage. This is ordinary electrics — power, ground, connector, bus, as in the lesson “No communication: the scan tool can’t see the modules”.

Secondary codes. The blog has a 2023 Haval after an off-road trip: codes in almost every module, including ESP, automatic braking and the front camera. After clearing and rechecking, only codes for lost communication with the AWD coupling remained, and the cause was a broken latch on its connector. Once the connector was repaired, the codes were gone.

Another example from the blog is a 2025 Subaru Outback: driver-assist warnings and many stored codes, including EyeSight. After clearing, one code stayed active — B2D04, front camera circuit or harness. The cause was a broken latch on the camera connector; the connector was repaired and the system started working.

Check the fuses first. And when codes light up for AWD, ESP, cameras and driver assists all at once after off-roading, I don’t rush to replace modules: I check the connectors, wiring, signs of moisture and physical damage first.
When calibration is needed

Replacing or removing the windshield on a car with a front camera, replacing the camera or its bracket. GM has required camera calibration after windshield replacement on all models since 2017; so does Honda, and the windshield must be genuine.

Removing, repairing or replacing the bumper, grille or badge near the radar, or a bent radar bracket after a minor impact. Honda, for example, requires radar aiming after a bumper cover repair within 300 mm of the radar.

Wheel alignment, suspension and steering repairs. Here the makes differ: the 2016 Subaru Legacy requires EyeSight camera calibration after an alignment and suspension work, while Honda doesn’t need it after an alignment unless the service information says so. The steering angle sensor is calibrated as in the lesson “Other systems and scan tool service functions”.
After a collision, an airbag deployment or replacement of the sensor itself. The exact list is in the manufacturer’s service information for that car: it outranks any general rules.

Why not “by eye”: in IIHS tests published in 2018, a Honda Civic camera that was 0.6° off misjudged the distance to the lane line by up to 69 cm (27 in). In an automatic braking test from about 40 km/h (25 mph), the car with that camera started braking later and hit the target at about 32 km/h (20 mph). A level and a tape measure can’t reach that precision — it takes the equipment and the manufacturer’s procedure.
Static and dynamic calibration

Static, in the bay: targets are set at the distance and height given in the procedure, square to the car’s centerline. You need a level floor, glare-free lighting, tire pressures per the placard, fuel and load as required, an empty cabin and trunk, and sound suspension.

Dynamic, on the road: the scan tool puts the system into calibration mode, and the car is driven at a set speed on a road with clear markings and moderate traffic. In snow, rain or on worn markings it may not complete.
Some makes require both in turn — static first, then dynamic; others let you choose one.

You need a scan tool or software that supports this make and its calibration function, plus a battery maintainer during the procedure, as in the lesson “Scan tools and adapters: what to choose and how to connect”.

Don’t clear calibration codes to turn off a warning light, and don’t set sensors “by eye”. An uncalibrated system may brake for no reason, fail to brake for an obstacle or steer the car out of its lane. If you don’t have the equipment, tell the customer honestly, send them to a dealer or a specialist calibration shop, and note in the report which system needs calibration and why.

Emission systems with a scan tool: catalytic converter, EVAP, EGR, secondary air and Mode 06

How to take an emissions code all the way to a repair: Mode 06 and a monitor on the edge, the causes of P0420, EVAP leaks and the smoke machine, checking EGR and secondary air — and what to tell a customer who asks you to “delete” a system.

Emission system codes are the P04xx group, as in the lesson “Trouble codes: statuses, freeze frame and root cause”: catalytic converter, evaporative emissions (EVAP), exhaust gas recirculation (EGR), secondary air. With these codes the car usually still drives, and the customer asks you to “just clear it” or “delete” it. But behind every code there is a cause you can find with a scan tool and a meter: misfires, mixture, a leak, carbon, a weak pump. Readiness monitors are covered in the lesson “The scan tool diagnostic procedure”, oxygen sensors and trims in “Fuel trims and oxygen sensors”, and valve control in “Actuator tests”. Here — how to take an emissions code all the way to a repair.
Mode 06: how far from a code

Readiness monitors only say “tested” or “not yet”. The results of the tests themselves are stored in Mode 06, found in the scan tool’s generic OBD-II section. For each test it shows a value, a minimum and maximum limit, and a “passed” or “failed” mark.
A code sets when the value goes past the limit. Mode 06 shows how much margin is left: the test passed, but the value is right at the edge — a reason to warn the customer before the light comes on.

Compare the value with its own limits, not with another car: units and scaling differ between makes. On CAN vehicles the tests are labeled to a standard — catalyst, EGR, EVAP, secondary air, O2 sensors, misfires by cylinder; on older cars the test names come from the manufacturer’s data. Not every car supports Mode 06.
The module keeps the result of the latest test even after the ignition is switched off, but clearing the codes erases the Mode 06 results too. So look at them before you clear anything.
After the repair, let the car complete a drive cycle and compare again: the value should move away from the limit. That way the repair is proven with a number, not just a light that went out.

Catalytic converter: P0420 is a consequence, not a diagnosis

The module judges the converter by the downstream O2 sensor: a healthy converter stores oxygen and the downstream sensor stays steady, while a worn one lets the upstream sensor’s swings through — see the lesson “Fuel trims and oxygen sensors”. Many modules also test actively: they briefly richen and lean the mixture and see how long the downstream sensor takes to respond. P0420 and P0430 mean catalyst efficiency below threshold, bank 1 and bank 2; P0421 and P0431 are the same for the warm-up converter closest to the engine. The catalyst monitor only runs under its own conditions, so “the code didn’t come back after clearing” proves nothing. On a 2007 Mitsubishi Outlander with P0421 and P0431, the codes didn’t return for 20 minutes after clearing; the oxygen sensors weren’t replaced on the strength of these codes, and the owner was sent to have the converters and exhaust checked (details on the blog: “Mitsubishi Outlander 2007 — Check Engine, codes P0421 and P0431”).
Save the codes, freeze frame and Mode 06, and scan all modules.

Fix whatever is killing the converter: misfires, a mixture that’s too rich or too lean, oil or coolant consumption. P0420 next to P0300 or P0171 is a consequence. On a 2005 Toyota RAV4, P0171 was set along with P0420, and the advice was to find the cause of the lean mixture first (details on the blog: “Toyota RAV4 2005 code P0125”).
Check the exhaust upstream of the downstream sensor: a leak through a burnt-out spot or a gasket feeds the sensor extra oxygen and spoils the test.
Check the sensors themselves on a warm engine: a lazy or stuck downstream sensor means repairing the sensor, not the converter.
Compare the banks in Mode 06: the worn converter’s test is closer to the limit.

If everything else is fine, it’s the converter: melted, clogged or “poisoned”. A clogged one also chokes the engine; exhaust back pressure is checked by an exhaust specialist. After the repair — a drive cycle and Mode 06 again.
EVAP: leaks and purge

EVAP keeps gasoline vapor out of the air: it goes from the tank into the canister — a container of charcoal — and while driving the module opens the purge valve so the engine draws the vapor into the intake and burns it. The vent valve connects the canister to the atmosphere; to test for leaks the module closes it and watches the tank pressure.

Codes: P0455 — large leak, P0442 — small, P0456 — very small; P0441 — incorrect purge flow, P0443 — purge valve circuit, P0446 — vent valve performance. US rules require on-board diagnostics to find a leak about 0.5 mm (0.020 inch) across — too small to see by eye.

Start with the simple things: the fuel cap and its seal, the filler neck, the valve connectors and hoses. On a 2022 Hyundai Tucson with a very small leak code, the first recommendation was to replace the fuel cap (details on the blog: “Hyundai Tucson 2022 — code P04567A”).

Then the scan tool: test the purge and vent valves and watch the tank pressure in live data — a single click from the valve isn’t enough. A purge valve stuck open is a vacuum leak into the intake: the idle hunts and the engine is hard to start after refueling.

If the valves and sensors are fine, look for the leak with a smoke machine. A 2025 Toyota Grand Highlander had large-leak codes after a collision, but the pump and valves passed their tests — the owner was advised to have the lines and connections checked for leaks (details on the blog: “Toyota Grand Highlander 2025 — diagnostics”).

Gasoline vapor burns and explodes. Feed smoke into EVAP only with a smoke machine made for this system, at the low pressure its instructions specify; compressed shop air is never fed into the tank. No flames or smoking nearby, a ventilated area, engine off.
EGR and secondary air

EGR returns part of the exhaust to the intake to lower combustion temperature and nitrogen oxide emissions. P0401 — not enough flow: most often carbon in the valve and passages. P0402 — too much flow: the valve doesn’t close, the idle is rough and the engine stalls.

Modules check the flow in different ways: by the jump in intake pressure when they open the valve during engine braking, or with a temperature or differential pressure sensor — it depends on the car. Compare the commanded and actual valve position as in the lesson “Actuator tests”: if the valve moves but there’s a flow code, it’s most likely carbon in the passages.

Secondary air only works after a cold start: a pump blows air into the exhaust to warm up the converter faster. The module checks the system with the upstream O2 sensor — it should read “lean” — or with the system’s pressure sensor. Codes: P0410 — system, P0411 — incorrect flow, P0418 — pump relay circuit.

The pump is switched through its own relay and fuse — check those first. Common failures: the pump seized from moisture, or the valve won’t open. Test it with the scan tool on a cold engine: you hear the pump, and the upstream sensor goes “lean”.
The customer asks to “delete” it

Requests to “cut out the converter”, “block off the EGR” or “disable” a system in software are common. We don’t do this, and we explain to the customer why. A code is a signal about a cause: misfires, mixture, carbon, a leak. “Deleting” the system doesn’t cure the cause, it hides it: the misfires or rich mixture remain and the carbon keeps building up. The car no longer meets its emissions class, emissions go up, and at inspection the exhaust is checked with a gas analyzer — a 2011 Toyota Tundra failed it on CO (details on the blog: “Toyota Tundra 2011 fails inspection on CO”). The law and the technician’s liability are covered in the lesson “Adaptations and resets”. Offer an honest repair: find the cause, clean or replace the valve, fit a suitable new converter and prove the result with the monitors and Mode 06.

With P0420 I don’t replace the converter on the strength of the code alone. First I look at misfires, fuel trims and the exhaust before the downstream sensor: if you don’t remove the cause, a new converter will be ruined the same way.
Mode 06 shows each test’s value and limits: a test on the edge is visible before a code sets. Check it before clearing.
P0420 is a consequence: misfires, mixture, exhaust and O2 sensors first, the converter last.

EGR and secondary air are checked with scan tool tests and live data; “deleting” is not a repair, and we don’t do it.

Common Rail diesel and SCR with a scan tool — no deletes

What to check in a diesel’s live data — target and actual rail pressure, the metering valve, injector corrections — where the electrician’s job ends, how to check the SCR with the NOx sensors, AdBlue quality and tests, and why we don’t fit emulators.

In a Common Rail system the high-pressure pump feeds fuel into a common rail at high pressure, and the ECU opens the injectors with electrical pulses. Many diesels — especially Euro 4 and newer trucks — also have SCR in the exhaust: AdBlue is injected into the exhaust, and the catalyst turns nitrogen oxides into nitrogen and water. Both systems are electronic, and the scan tool sees inside them. J1939 codes are covered in the lesson “Trucks and heavy equipment: a 24 V scan tool”, injector codes and DPF regeneration in “Other systems and scan tool service functions”, and per-cylinder corrections in “Engine tests with a scan tool: compression, balance, misfires, timing”. Here — how to find the cause from live data and where the electrician’s job ends.
Common Rail: what to check in live data

Rail pressure — target and actual. The ECU sets the pressure from rpm and load, the rail sensor reports how much there really is, and the actual should follow the target: in a healthy system the difference is usually up to 30–50 bar. Typical guidelines: at least 200 bar while cranking to start, from 250 bar at warm idle, more than 1,000 bar under load; modern systems go up to 2,700 bar. Guidelines are on the “Sensors” tab, exact figures in the manufacturer’s data. The scan tool may show MPa: 1 MPa = 10 bar.

The metering valve on the high-pressure pump and the pressure regulator on the rail are how the ECU holds pressure; some systems have one of them, others both. The scan tool shows their current or duty cycle. Compare with the manufacturer’s data or a healthy vehicle with the same engine: if the valve is at its limit and the pressure won’t build, the ECU is short of fuel.

The rail pressure sensor is usually a three-wire sensor with a 5 V supply: with no pressure the signal is about 0.5 V, and it rises with pressure. With the engine off and the pressure bled away, the scan tool should read close to zero; hundreds of bar on a stopped engine means the sensor or its circuit.

Injector corrections per cylinder: if one is at its limit, check that injector and the cylinder’s compression. Injector codes are entered with the scan tool after replacement — see the lesson “Other systems and scan tool service functions”.
Boost and airflow: black smoke and loss of power can come from the air side too, not just the fuel.

Target and actual: reading the gap

Actual below target when starting or under load — P0087, pressure too low. Look at the supply: fuel in the tank, air in the system, a clogged filter, the lift pump, the high-pressure pump, injectors leaking into the return. A Mercedes Sprinter stalled when it was running out of fuel: a low rail pressure code was stored, and after a few cranks the fuel was drawn through and the engine started (details on the blog: “Mercedes Sprinter stalled and won’t start”).

No pressure at all — check the high-pressure pump and its valves. On a 2012 MAN TGX the pump delivered no fuel: its pressure relief valve was stuck open; after it was restored and the system bled, the engine started (details on the blog: “MAN TGX 2012 wouldn’t start — the high-pressure pump wasn’t pumping”).

Actual above target or jumping — P0088, pressure too high: the metering valve, the regulator, the sensor or their wiring. Check the sensor’s 5 V supply and ground and look at its signal with an oscilloscope.

Target and actual match, but the engine smokes — pressure isn’t the problem, look at the injectors and air. On an excavator with a Cummins engine, target and actual matched, but black smoke and imbalance remained — the advice was to have the injectors checked by fuel injection specialists (details on the blog: “Excavator with a Cummins engine — black smoke”).

Where the electrician’s job ends

An electrician with a scan tool finds the direction: data, codes, wiring, connectors, sensors, power to the valves. Wiring and connectors are the electrician’s to fix: on a 2018 bus, misfiring and loss of power came from a damaged terminal in an injector connector — after repinning, the SPN 653 code went away (details on the blog: “Bus diagnostics, 2018 — fixing SPN 653”). But bench-testing injectors, measuring return flow — how much fuel an injector leaks back — repairing the high-pressure pump and measuring compression are jobs for a fuel injection specialist and an engine mechanic. As in the lesson “Compression and mechanicals: when the electrics aren’t to blame”: write down your measurements honestly and pass the vehicle on.

Rail pressure is hundreds to thousands of bar. Don’t loosen high-pressure lines or the sensor with the engine running or right after it stops: wait for the pressure to drop — the time is in the manual. A jet of fuel at this pressure goes through skin — a serious injury, see a doctor at once. Look for leaks with your eyes and a piece of cardboard, never your hand; no smoking nearby.
SCR and AdBlue: repair, not an emulator

Components: the AdBlue tank with level, temperature and often quality sensors, tank and line heaters, the pump, the dosing injector in the exhaust pipe, the SCR catalyst, NOx sensors before and after it, and exhaust temperature sensors.

The main check is the NOx sensors. On a warm, healthy SCR, NOx after the catalyst is several times lower than before it: for example, 300 ppm before and about 30 after — roughly 90 %. If “after” is almost equal to “before”, the SCR isn’t working (P20EE; on trucks under J1939 — SPN 4364). NOx sensors start measuring once they’re warm: zeros on a cold engine aren’t a fault.

Fluid quality: AdBlue is a 32.5 % urea solution (tolerance 31.8–33.2 %), checked with a refractometer. Diluted fluid causes quality and efficiency codes. A 2022 DAF XF 106 had an active low AdBlue concentration code and a 20 km/h limit; after a reset the limit was lifted, but the concentration still has to be checked or the code will come back (details on the blog: “DAF XF 106 2022 — 20 km/h limit, AdBlue codes”).

Scan tool tests: pump pressure (P20E8 — AdBlue pressure too low), a dosing test into a measuring container — the volume is compared with the target — and a heater test. White crystals on the dosing injector and in the pipe are a sign of poor spray or poor fluid.

Winter: AdBlue freezes at about −11 °C, which is why there are heaters. A heater fault means power, relay, fuse, connector and the heater’s resistance per the manufacturer’s data. After the engine stops, many trucks need time for the pump to empty AdBlue from the lines: don’t turn off the battery master switch right away, wait the time given in the vehicle’s manual — often about 80 seconds.

Not everything is complicated: on a 2025 Sinotruk the AdBlue warning was due to a low level — after topping up it went away (details on the blog: “Sinotruk 2025 — computer diagnostics”). For more on the fluid itself, see the app’s “AdBlue” section.

We don’t fit AdBlue emulators or “disable” SCR, EGR or the DPF in software — why is explained in the lessons “Adaptations and resets” and “Trucks and heavy equipment: a 24 V scan tool”. Explain it simply to the customer: a code is a signal about a specific fault that can be found — a NOx sensor, the pump, a heater, the dosing injector, wiring or bad fluid. An emulator doesn’t fix it, it hides it; without SCR there are several times more nitrogen oxides in the exhaust, and the vehicle no longer meets its emissions class. Finding the cause is often cheaper than it seems: top up or replace the fluid, repair a connector, replace one sensor.
If a truck has an AdBlue heater fault, I check the heater fuses and relays first, and only then the heaters themselves and the pump.

Won’t start: a step-by-step check from the battery to the spark

What a technician does, in order, when a car won’t start: battery and grounds, starter, cranking speed, immobilizer, fuel, injectors, spark and mechanicals — with measurements, typical figures and cases from Oleg’s blog.

The driver lesson “Why the car won’t start” gives four steps you can do by ear and by eye. A technician needs more: every step needs a measurement with a number that says “OK” or “not OK”, and only then comes the next step. Start by asking what happens when the key is turned — silence, a click, slow or brisk cranking, “catches and dies” — and whether the dash lights up. The general method is in the lesson “Troubleshooting method and working with ECUs”; here it is applied to one complaint. On the phone I always start with the fuses. Then it depends on the symptom. A click but no cranking — a few firm taps with a hammer on the starter housing. An automatic that won’t crank in P — have them try N, with the brake pressed and the parking brake on. A silent fuel pump — a light tap on the bottom of the tank. If the car then starts, the part is worn: the starter, the range sensor or the pump needs checking and repair before it fails for good. On site, I still go step by step with measurements.
Steps 1–2. Battery, grounds and starter
Battery at rest — the car has sat, everything off: 12.4–12.9 V. Lower — charge and test it first, as in the lesson “Batteries for pros”: with a flat battery the other measurements tell you nothing.

Sag while cranking: probes on the battery posts — no lower than about 9.6 V. From the blog: a Kia Optima showed about 10 V with the ignition on and 7 V when cranking; on a Hyundai Bayon 2023 the starter wouldn’t crank and the interior lights didn’t dim, yet the battery sagged to 9 V. Both owners were advised to replace the battery: “the lights don’t dim” is no substitute for a measurement.

Losses under load, while cranking: from the battery “+” post to starter terminal 30 — up to 0.5 V; from the starter housing to the battery “−” post — up to 0.2–0.3 V. More than that — look for a corroded clamp, ground strap or cable.

Silence with a charged battery — the interlocks: automatic selector in P or N, clutch pedal fully down, brake pressed on push-button cars. Then the starter fuse and relay, and the positive at terminal 50 while cranking — almost the same as at the battery. From the blog: a Nissan X-Trail 2021 wouldn’t crank when cold — the starter relay under the left headlight was to blame.

There’s a positive at 50, but the starter clicks or cranks slowly — the problem is the starter itself (the solenoid and its contact discs, the brushes) or the power circuit. Cranking current — with a clamp meter: usually around 100–200 A for gasoline passenger cars. High current and slow — mechanical; low current and slow — resistance in the circuit. Details are in the lesson “Starter motor: design and testing”.
Steps 3–4. Cranking speed, shaft sensors and the immobilizer

If the starter cranks briskly, connect the scan tool and watch engine speed in live data while cranking: usually about 150–250 rpm. Zero while the starter turns — the ECU doesn’t see the crankshaft signal and gives neither injection nor spark; P0335, crankshaft position sensor circuit, is often stored.

P0340 — camshaft sensor circuit: depending on the system, the engine takes longer to start or doesn’t start at all. Shaft sensor signals are checked with an oscilloscope while cranking — see the lesson “Oscilloscope: seeing the signal”.

Shaft sensor codes may be left over from earlier glitches: record them, clear them and crank again — did they come back? From the blog: a Kia Soul 2009 had P0343 and P0336; after clearing they didn’t return, and the real reason it wouldn’t start was the fuel pump — it was getting power but not running.

Immobilizer: the key or lock symbol flashes; the engine doesn’t catch, or catches and dies after 1–2 seconds; the ECU has an immobilizer code or no communication with the immobilizer module. Then follow the lesson “Immobilizers & keys”: battery, spare key, interference on the key ring, fuses, power and ground of the module and antenna. We never disable or bypass the immobilizer, and we program keys only with the vehicle’s documents.

The dash stays dark or the scan tool can’t see the engine ECU — check power: fuses, ignition switch, main relay, ECU grounds (lesson “Fuel injection, ECU power and grounds”). From the blog: on a Lexus GS300 the instrument panel stayed dark with the ignition on, the starter cranked but the engine wouldn’t start — a faulty ignition switch contact group wasn’t passing power to some of the systems.

Step 5. Fuel

First the obvious — is there fuel in the tank? Then the prime: on many cars the pump runs for 2–3 seconds when the ignition is switched on and stops if the ECU sees no rotation. Not on all of them, though: on the Toyota Corolla 2014 from the blog the pump only comes on while cranking — silence with the ignition on is normal there. That car wouldn’t start because of a defective new fuel filter: there was no pressure.

If the pump is silent — fuse and relay, then the positive and ground at the pump connector under load, and the current with a clamp meter. From the blog: on a Nissan Patrol 2015 the fuse, relay and alarm cut-off were fine and voltage reached the pump module, but the positive contact in the module itself and the mating connector had burned.

Pressure — with a gauge on the fuel rail test port or through an adapter in the line. Multipoint (port) injection engines usually run about 2.5–4.5 bar (35–65 psi); the exact spec is in the manual. After shutdown the pressure should hold for a while; if it drops quickly, look for a leak: the pump check valve, the pressure regulator, an injector. With direct injection, rail pressure after the high-pressure pump is tens of bar even while cranking: read it with the scan tool — a low-pressure gauge doesn’t go there.

From the blog: a Toyota Hiace 2018 had code P1200 — per the scan tool’s description, the fuel pump control circuit or its relay. The code was cleared and didn’t return; voltage was reaching the pump, yet the pump only started after a light knock on the fuel module cover. Conclusion: replace the pump and check the module contacts.
Steps 6–7. Injector pulse and spark

Injector pulse — while cranking, with a dedicated injector noid light plugged into the harness connector in place of the injector, or with an oscilloscope. Don’t connect an ordinary test lamp to ECU pins or sensor circuits — as in the lesson “Fuel injection, ECU power and grounds”.

While cranking, the scan tool shows injection pulse width — that’s the ECU’s command, not proof the injector opened. No pulse on any injector — main relay, ECU power and grounds, crankshaft signal, immobilizer; none on one injector — its wire and its ECU pin.

Spark — only with a spark tester: put the removed coil or the plug wire on the tester, clip the tester to engine ground, crank briefly. A steady spark across the gap on every cylinder means the ignition works. Disable the injectors or the pump as the manual describes while you test, so fuel doesn’t flood the cylinders.

No spark on any coil — crankshaft sensor, ECU power and grounds, the coil fuse, immobilizer. From the blog: a Honda CR-V 1998 had no spark because of the igniter; the owner replaced it himself and mounted it on the distributor housing incorrectly — the ECU output transistor was damaged and the ECU had to be repaired.

Crank for no more than 10 seconds at a time, with 30–60 second pauses, and never bridge terminals 30 and 50 with a screwdriver: that bypasses the interlocks, and a car in gear will drive off. The fuel line is under pressure: relieve it as the manual describes, keep a fire extinguisher at hand, no sparks or flames. Don’t test for spark “to ground” or hold a lead in your hand: the secondary circuit carries tens of thousands of volts. Keep your hands and test leads away from the belts and the fan — the engine may start.
Step 8. When it’s mechanical

The starter cranks briskly, the scan tool shows engine speed, the key is recognized, pressure is in spec, there are injector pulses and spark — and the engine still won’t catch: check the mechanicals. Clues: an uneven cranking sound, cranking that’s too easy, camshaft/crankshaft correlation codes. Relative compression and timing with a scan tool — lesson “Engine tests with a scan tool: compression, balance, misfires, timing”; a compression gauge test — lesson “Compression and mechanicals: when the electrics aren’t to blame”. If it’s confirmed, tell the customer honestly and hand the car to an engine mechanic: you can’t fix mechanical faults with electrics.

Add-on equipment: fog lights, light bars, auxiliary lights — wiring them right

The wiring diagram for auxiliary lights through a relay with a fuse at the battery, calculating current, fuse rating, wire gauge and voltage drop, what’s special about LED light bars, routing in tape and split loom with rubber grommets where wires pass through metal — and what the rules in Kazakhstan allow.

Fog lights, roof-mounted light bars, auxiliary headlights, work lights on a truck — common jobs for an auto electrician and a common reason for calls after a “garage” install. From the blog: fog lights are very often wired straight through the switch, with no relay and no fuse — the wiring melts, contacts overheat, switches burn out. Simple rules for owners are in the drivers’ course lesson “Dashcam, head unit, lights: wiring them right,” how a relay works is in “Relays and control circuits,” and connections are in “Wiring and connector repair.” This lesson is the technician’s job: the diagram, the calculation and the routing, after which nothing overheats or chafes.
The diagram: power circuit and control circuit

Power circuit: battery positive → fuse right at the terminal → relay terminal 30 → terminal 87 → lights wired in parallel → ground. The wire is sized by the calculation below and kept as short as possible.

Control circuit: the cabin switch only energizes the relay coil — positive to 86 through the switch, 85 to ground. The coil draws a fraction of an amp, so the switch and its thin wire don’t heat up. A relay with a diode is polarized — as in the lesson “Relays and control circuits.”

Positive to the switch: for fog lights, from the parking light circuit, because under the Kazakhstan Traffic Rules they come on only with the parking lights on. Auxiliary high beams and a light bar are best controlled from the high-beam circuit: switch to low beam for an oncoming car, and they go off too.
An illuminated switch: the backlight comes from the instrument lighting or parking light circuit, and the indicator shows the driver the lights are on.
Ground is a separate wire of the same gauge as the positive, with a ring terminal to clean metal under a factory bolt or to the battery negative. A bad ground means dim light and flicker.
The relay has contacts rated with a margin and is mounted in a dry spot; the fuse holder is sealed, with a cover.

The calculation: current, fuse, wire, voltage drop

Current: I = P / U; calculate at 12 V — that builds in a margin. Two 55 W fog lights: 110 / 12 ≈ 9 A. A 180 W light bar: 180 / 12 = 15 A. The advertised power of cheap products often doesn’t match the real one — measure the current with a DC clamp meter and calculate from the reading.

The fuse protects the wire: the rating is about 1.25 times the working current, rounded up to a standard value, and no more than the wire can carry. For a pair of fog lights — 15 A, for a 15 A light bar — 20 A.

Gauge is chosen by the fuse and the length; the table is in the lesson “Dashcam, head unit, lights.” For fog lights on a 15 A fuse — 2.5 mm², for a light bar on 20 A — 4 mm². The wire is stranded copper, not copper-clad aluminum (CCA).

Check by voltage drop: copper wire resistance R = 0.0175 × L / S (Ω; L is the length in meters, S the cross-section in mm²), drop ΔU = I × R. A pair of fog lights, 9 A, 5 m positive wire: 1.5 mm² — 0.53 V, 2.5 mm² — 0.32 V. A light bar, 15 A, 5 m of 4 mm² wire — about 0.33 V. The target, as in the lesson “Electricity in the car”: up to 0.5 V on the positive side and up to 0.2–0.3 V on ground. If the ground runs as a wire back to the battery, calculate it too.
A halogen bulb is very sensitive to voltage: every half volt lost noticeably reduces the light, and a wire at its limit also heats up.

Inrush current: a cold halogen filament draws several times its working current for the first fraction of a second, and LED light bars and LED headlights have capacitors at the driver input — a short current surge at switch-on. So the relay gets contacts rated with a margin, connections are crimped, and the fuse is sized by calculation, not cut to the bone. If it blows at switch-on with no short, measure the real current with a clamp meter.

I never wire high-power lights straight through the switch: only a relay and a fuse near the battery, and I don’t skimp on the wiring. I use a quality fuse — a cheap one of unknown make may not blow at its rating but melt along with its holder. And if both fog lights later go out at once, I check the fuse, the relay and the power feed first; if only one is out, it’s almost always the bulb or a contact.
Routing: tape, split loom, rubber grommets
Before you start, disconnect the battery negative terminal. Route along the factory harnesses: there the wire is already protected from heat and movement, just like the factory one.

The wire goes in tape and in split loom. Tape depends on the location: cloth tape in the cabin, since it doesn’t squeak or rattle; PVC under the hood, since it isn’t bothered by moisture. Tape bundles and protects the harness but doesn’t insulate a joint — joints get heat shrink, as in the lesson “Wiring and connector repair.”

Split loom runs the full length under the hood, under the floor and anywhere the wire could rub; under the hood it’s heat-resistant and sized with room to spare. Secure the loom too and tape its ends: loose loom chafes the wire itself and collects dirt.

Through metal — only through rubber grommets. The factory firewall grommet is best: you pierce the rubber, not the metal. If you drill, first check what’s behind the panel, then deburr the hole, paint the edge against rust, and fit a grommet of the right size plus sealant. Without a grommet, vibration lets the edge cut through the loom and insulation down to the copper — a short to ground and a fire risk.

Secure it with zip ties to the factory harnesses, usually every 20–30 cm, so the wire doesn’t flop around. Don’t tie it to fuel or brake lines; keep it away from the exhaust manifold, turbo and other hot parts, and from the belt, fan, steering shaft and suspension. Where parts move — doors, hood, a truck’s tilt cab — leave a service loop with slack, in loom.
Under the hood and outside: sealed connectors with a seal on every wire and adhesive-lined heat shrink; mount the relay terminals down so water doesn’t sit in the socket.

From the blog: on a 2023 KamAZ, the wires were pinched during an earlier heater fan replacement, and vibration wore through the insulation — a short to ground, and the heater fuse kept blowing. On a 2023 Fendt combine, a control wire chafed against its protective loom — an open circuit; it was repaired with solder and heat shrink, laid back in loom and secured with ties so it wouldn’t chafe again.

A chafed positive wire shorts to the body. If the fuse sits at the lights or there’s no fuse at all, the whole wire from the battery burns — that’s a fire. So the fuse goes right at the terminal, rated for the wire. If it blows, look for the short; never fit a “bigger” fuse or a jumper in its place. Work with the battery negative disconnected, and drill only after making sure there are no wires, lines or tank behind the panel.
Lighting modules, CAN and LED interference

If the lights are switched by the body control module or a lighting module (the lesson “Module-controlled and CAN lighting”), you never splice into the CAN bus — not for power, not for a “signal”: codes will appear and the car may not start. Don’t load module outputs with extra lights either: an output is designed for its own bulb, monitors its current, and on overload it shuts off or burns out. Auxiliary lights go only through their own relay fed from the battery.

On these cars the parking light wire often comes from a PWM module output — check it with an oscilloscope. On PWM the relay coil may chatter, and the module may log a code. Then look for the factory provision: many cars have a fog light connector in the harness, and the function is enabled with a scan tool — per the service manual.

From the blog: on a Toyota Highlander, the right turn signal stayed on constantly and the hazard switch made no difference; after the installed alarm’s connectors were unplugged, the fault went away. Aftermarket equipment in the lighting circuits is the first thing to check.

Interference: an LED driver is a switching converter, and a cheap one without filtering is “noisy” — when the light bar comes on, the radio hisses or drops out. What helps: a product with a conformity mark (the letter E with a country number), a solid ground, wires kept away from the antenna cable, and ferrite rings on the power leads at the driver. If that doesn’t help, replace the product.

A 24 V truck: lights and light bars rated for 24 V or with a suitable supply range per their spec sheet, and a relay with a 24 V coil; at the same power the current is half, as in the lesson “Trucks: the 24 V system and the J1939 bus.”
What the rules in Kazakhstan allow

Kazakhstan Traffic Rules: fog lights are switched on with the parking lights on (clause 133). They’re used in poor visibility — on their own or with low or high beams — and in the dark on unlit roads together with low or high beams (clause 132).
Spotlights and search lights — only outside populated areas and with no oncoming traffic (clause 135). Rear fog lights are not wired to the brake lights (clause 136).

The list of defects that prohibit operating a vehicle: the number, type, color, placement and operating mode of exterior lights must match the vehicle’s design (chapter 3, clause 11); no red lights at the front, and no white at the rear except reverse lights and the license plate light (clause 16).

Installing equipment not provided for in the design that affects road safety is a modification (clause 46 of the list). According to a police explanation (2025), any change to the lighting system counts as a modification; without registering it, the fine is under Article 590, part 7 of the Administrative Offenses Code. Discuss a light bar or lights that the model wasn’t designed with before the job, and check the registration procedure with the police.

The rules are per Ministry of Internal Affairs order No. 534 of 30.06.2023 (the Traffic Rules and the Basic Provisions for Admitting Vehicles to Operation). Before the job, check the current wording at adilet.zan.kz.

Auxiliary lights go only through a relay: the switch energizes the coil (a fraction of an amp), the light current flows from the battery through a fuse right at the terminal; ground is a separate wire to clean metal.

Calculation: I = P / U, the fuse about 1.25 × I up to a standard value and matched to the wire, drop ΔU = I × 0.0175 × L / S — up to 0.5 V on the positive side. With LEDs, allow for inrush and check for interference.

Routing: the wire in tape (cloth in the cabin, PVC under the hood) and in split loom, through metal only via rubber grommets, zip-tied to the factory harnesses, away from hot and moving parts; sealed connectors and heat shrink under the hood.
On cars with a lighting module and CAN, don’t splice into the bus and don’t load module outputs. Fog lights come on with the parking lights, and unregistered auxiliary lighting is a modification.

The car won’t go to sleep: finding and removing the current draw

How a car goes to sleep step by step, what wakes it, how to spot a module that stays awake, find the draw quickly with a clamp and by fuse voltage drop, remove it and prove the result with a measurement — using Oleg’s 0.06 A limit.

Key-off current limits, waiting for the modules to sleep, connecting an ammeter without breaking the circuit and searching by fuse voltage drop were covered in the lesson “Parasitic draw: how to track it down”. This lesson is practice: how a car goes to sleep step by step, how to spot a module that stays awake, how to find and remove the draw quickly and how to prove to the customer that it’s gone.

My rule: once the car is asleep, the key-off current should ideally be 0.06 A (60 mA) or less. Any more and I look for the cause, even if the car still starts for now. On most passenger cars it’s 20–50 mA, as in the lesson “Parasitic draw”; if the manufacturer gives its own limit, I check against that. Do the math: 60 mA is about 1.4 Ah a day, and over two weeks parked about 20 Ah — a third of a 60 Ah battery.
How a car goes to sleep: current steps

Right after switching off and locking, the current is high — hundreds of milliamps or even amps: modules are still running, the ECU holds the main relay, lights are on, the cooling fan may keep running.
Then the current drops in steps: the lights go out, comfort and infotainment modules fall asleep, the bus goes quiet. Each step is a module or a group of modules going to sleep.

The last step is the key-off current: module memory, the clock, the key fob receiver, the alarm. That’s what you compare with the limit. How long to wait is in the manual: some cars need just a few minutes, others, according to Pico Technology, 30 minutes to 2 hours.

On a BMW, for example, most modules should be asleep within the first 16 minutes, and the system flags any module still awake at 20 minutes as a sleep-mode preventer (“Energy Management”, The Bimmer Pub, 2016).

Sleeping modules sometimes wake briefly on their own — to check the battery or check in (telematics, a GSM alarm). Short spikes between long pauses are normal if the current between them is within the limit.

What wakes the car and how to spot a module that stays awake
Doors, hood and trunk — their switches; buttons and the key fob; a keyless-entry key near the car — move it well away.
An alarm with sensors and a GSM module, factory telematics, remote start — they wake on a schedule or on command.
Bus traffic: one module sends a message and the rest wake up. A connected scan tool wakes the bus too, so leave the diagnostic port alone while the car sleeps.

A drain can be intermittent (see the blog: “Why the battery goes flat overnight”): the module doesn’t stay awake every time. Then log the current for hours — a scope with a clamp — or measure several times.

The main sign of a module that stays awake is a step: the current dropped but got stuck at a few hundred milliamps and stays there for hours. A light or a dash cam gives the same kind of step, so look at the bus: put a scope on CAN-H and CAN-L to ground, at the diagnostic port or at a module. In sleep, both high-speed CAN wires sit near zero — the transceivers bias the lines to ground (Texas Instruments TCAN1042 data sheet). About 2.5 V with frames running means some module is holding the bus awake. Fault-tolerant body CAN has different sleep levels — see the manual. Connect the scan tool afterwards: it will wake the bus, but it shows the codes, and on some cars the energy management module records what kept the network awake.

Searching without taking things apart: the clamp and fuse voltage drop
Put a DC clamp meter around the battery negative cable; if several wires leave the terminal, enclose them all. Warm the clamp up and zero it before measuring — Pico suggests waiting 10 minutes.

Then use the same clamp along the harnesses: the positive feeds to the fuse boxes, the harness to the trunk or a door, add-on equipment wiring. Current in a harness tells you right away which way to go, and the car doesn’t wake up.
Clamp feed wires only: if a harness carries both the positive and the ground of the same load, the currents cancel and the clamp reads almost zero.

Fuse voltage drop: a millivoltmeter with 0.1 mV resolution on the test points on top. Current = drop ÷ fuse resistance. Littelfuse mini fuses are typically 7.42 mΩ at 10 A, so 1 mV ≈ 135 mA, and 17.75 mΩ at 5 A, so 1 mV ≈ 56 mA. Other ratings are in the picture.
The whole 0.06 A limit across one 10 A fuse is only 0.45 mV. That’s why you need a sensitive meter and a table from the maker of those particular fuses: other brands have different resistance.

If the fuses show nothing but the clamp on the negative still shows a drain, move to the heavy cables that have no fuse or one fuse for everything: alternator B+, the starter positive, high-current fusible links, amplifier and inverter cables run straight from the battery. Clamp B+ with the engine off: current there points to a shorted rectifier diode or the regulator, provided nothing else is fed from that cable (check the diagram). How to disconnect the alternator for the check is in the lesson “Parasitic draw”. A case from practice — a 2020 Hyundai Santa Fe (details in the blog: “Hyundai Santa Fe 2020 — excessive current draw”): the drain was about 14 A; after checking the charging system and the circuits and disconnecting modules one by one, the culprit turned out to be the alternator with an internal fault. It was replaced, and the follow-up measurement was normal.
Common culprits and how to fix them

Add-on equipment — an alarm, dash cam, amplifier, GPS tracker — wired to constant power or not shutting off. Fix: power it from the ignition (ACC or 15) through a fuse tap in a non-critical circuit, heavy loads through a relay switched by the ignition; for a dash cam with parking mode, a low-voltage cutoff per its instructions. How to wire it is in the course “For drivers”, lesson “Dashcam, head unit, lights: wiring them in properly”.
A stuck relay: a heater, pump or fan keeps running after shutdown. Fix: replace the relay with one of the same circuit and find out why it stuck — as in the lesson “Relays and control circuits”.
An alternator with a shorted diode — current through B+ with the engine off. Fix: repair or replace the alternator, then check charging.

Water in a connector or module: the module won’t sleep or “sees” a button as pressed. Fix: find where the water gets in (drains, seals), dry it out, clean the contacts, replace corroded terminals — as in the lesson “Wiring and connector repair”.

A module that stays awake for no visible reason: check its power, ground, inputs (switches) and codes. If the manufacturer has released a software update for it, install it only through official channels — the dealer or J2534 with official access, as in the lesson “Official reprogramming” of the course “Scan tool diagnostics”.
Trunk, glove box and underhood lights: the switch is broken or isn’t pressed, so the light stays on with the lid closed. Fix: adjust or replace the switch.

From practice (in the blog: “Finding a hidden current draw”): a faulty amplifier after an audio install — a constant 0.2 A drain; corroded alarm wires — the alarm didn’t fully cut power and the battery went flat in 2–3 days; an old power-window module — 0.1 A while switched off.
Checking after the repair and a record for the customer
Reassemble everything you took apart, close the doors and hood or latch the locks as for the first measurement; move the key away.
Let the car fall asleep again — at least as long as the first time — and measure the same way: same clamp, same cable.
0.06 A or less, or the manual’s limit — done. More than that — keep looking: there can be two culprits.
Check the battery and charging: after a deep discharge the battery may need replacing, and the alternator must stay in spec under load — as in the lesson “Charging system”.
Write it down for the customer: current before and after, how many minutes after locking you measured, what you found and what you did. If they come back, you’ll have something to compare with.

That’s how it was done on a Lexus LX 570 (details in the blog: “Lexus LX 570 — battery replacement, parasitic draw and alternator check”). The battery had been discharged to about 3 V. The terminals were cleaned and a new battery fitted — and the job didn’t stop there: once the modules were asleep the current was measured at 0.01 A (10 mA), and the alternator gave 14.1 V under load. A conclusion with numbers: no drain and no charging problem at the time of the check; the cause was the deeply discharged old battery.

While the ammeter is in series with the negative, don’t switch on the ignition, the lights or the starter. The alternator B+ cable and other heavy cables are always live at battery voltage: clamp only over the insulation, and disconnect wires only with the negative off. Never put jumpers in place of fuses, and never take power for add-on equipment from the airbag, ABS, engine ECU or fuel pump circuits.
Oleg’s limit: 0.06 A or less once the modules are asleep; more than that — find the cause. The exact limit is in the manual.
A car falls asleep in steps. Current stuck on a step plus about 2.5 V and frames on CAN means a module hasn’t gone to sleep. A scan tool wakes the bus — connect it afterwards.

Search without taking things apart: clamp on the negative and along the harnesses, then fuse voltage drop — current = mV ÷ resistance. Nothing there — check alternator B+, the starter and heavy cables.
Once the cause is fixed, let the car sleep again, measure the same way and record the before-and-after current for the customer.

What a sole proprietor on the simplified regime must keep
Which documents and records a sole proprietor (IP) on the simplified regime keeps, when full accounting books are required, what to keep records in, and why this course is only for your own IP.

A sole proprietor on the simplified regime doesn’t have to hire a bookkeeper or keep full accounting books until income reaches a threshold. But “keeping nothing” isn’t an option either: documents for every job, income records, the tax return and payments are on you. This course shows how to handle all of it yourself, using an auto electrician’s repair shop in Almaty as the example.
Information based on Kazakhstan law as of October 26, 2026. This is not legal or tax advice: rules change — check kgd.gov.kz and the Tax Code, or ask your local tax office (UGD).
This course is for your own IP

This course teaches you to keep the books of your own IP. On the simplified regime you can’t keep books for others for a fee: “Accounting or audit activities” (OKED 69201, 69202, 69205) is item 23 of the list of activities barred from the simplified regime (Government Resolution No. 970 of November 14, 2025). Tax consulting (OKED 69203) is item 22 of the same list.

Inventory counts — do them: compare what your documents show with what you actually have, such as parts on the shelf.

An IP on the simplified regime may skip accounting books and financial statements if all of these hold: annual income is at most 135,000 MCI (₸583,875,000 in 2026), the IP isn’t registered for VAT, and it isn’t a natural monopoly. The basis is the Law “On Accounting and Financial Reporting” (Art. 2(2)(1)) and Art. 202(4) of the Tax Code; the State Revenue Committee (KGD) explains it the same way. Simplified-regime taxpayers aren’t registered for VAT (Art. 99 of the Tax Code), so for a repair shop the key condition is income.

If income since the start of the year goes over the threshold, accounting books are kept from the month after the month it was crossed. For a small shop that’s far off: at ₸4,000,000 a month, the year comes to ₸48,000,000 — about 8% of the threshold.

When a simplified-regime IP pays for themselves and their employees, when to file Form 910.00 and pay its tax, when to file Form 200.00, and what happens if you miss a deadline.

A simplified-regime IP has three rhythms of deadlines: monthly payments, Form 910.00 and its tax every half-year, and Form 200.00 every quarter if you have employees. The dates below follow the KGD tax calendar for 2026. It’s handy to enter them once in your phone calendar with reminders.

The deadlines here are for the simplified regime. Anyone who was on the simplified regime in 2025 and didn’t file the notice of the applied tax regime between January 1 and March 1, 2026 was moved to the general regime (OUR) from January 1, 2026 — with different forms and deadlines. What counts as income

Which money counts as a shop’s income for Form 910.00 — cash, card, QR, transfers from companies and to a personal card; how to handle refunds and prepayments; and why the register must match the return.

On the simplified regime, tax is calculated from income, so the main thing in your records is not to miss a single receipt and not to report anything extra. Using an auto electrician’s shop in Almaty, let’s see what money counts as income for Form 910.00.
Income — with no deduction for expenses

On the simplified regime, the tax base is income for the half-year. Expenses — parts, bay rent, tools — aren’t deducted from it. Only adjustments reduce income: a refund to a customer, a discount, a price change. That’s what Article 724 of the Tax Code says; we checked its text against a copy of the code in open sources — confirm the details with your local tax office.

Tax = income × rate. The base rate is 4%, and the local maslikhat (council) can change it. For Almaty, accounting websites report a 3% rate for 2026 (maslikhat decision No. 256 of November 28, 2025); we haven’t checked the text of the decision — confirm the rate with your local tax office.
What goes into income
Cash for repairs and diagnostics — with a fiscal receipt from the cash register (KKM).
Card and QR payments (Kaspi Pay and others) — income too, and also with a fiscal receipt.
Transfers from companies and IPs — fleets, businesses — to the IP account under an invoice and act; you issue ESFs for them.
Money for work sent to the mechanic’s personal card is IP income too. Taking payment this way is a risk (see below).

About the register: according to clarifications in open sources (accounting websites, 2025–2026), a fiscal receipt is needed for cash, card and QR payments, and a Kaspi bank receipt doesn’t count as fiscal; a transfer from a company’s bank account under an invoice usually doesn’t require a KKM receipt. Confirm with your local tax office.

Refunds and prepayments

Refunds. If a customer rejects the work and you return the money, the refund reduces income (an adjustment under Article 724). Document it: if the payment went through the register, process the refund through the register and keep the receipt.

Prepayments. Which half-year an advance belongs to — by payment date or by the date of the act — isn’t answered in the official 2026 KGD clarifications we found. If you take prepayments, for example for parts on order, confirm this with your local tax office.
The register and the return must match

Everything you printed a fiscal receipt for is income. Before filing Form 910.00, check: the half-year’s KKM receipts plus transfers from companies minus refunds equals the income on the return. If Form 910.00 shows less, that’s underreported income; missed income is fixed with an amended return (lesson 8).

The ISNA account, EDS, and your personal account
Where an IP files returns and notices, how to work in the taxpayer account with your own EDS, why to read tax office messages, and how to spot debt or an overpayment in your personal account.

An IP files returns, notices, and applications with the tax office electronically and signs them with their own EDS. The main place for this is the ISNA taxpayer account. Let’s see what to look for there and how to check once a month that you owe nothing. The screens in this lesson are teaching mockups: the real account looks roughly like this, and section names may change.
Where documents are filed
The ISNA taxpayer account — returns, notices, applications. Per explanations in public sources, use the new account and stop using the old one.
E-Salyq Business — the KGD mobile app; per accounting portals (mybuh.kz, July 1, 2026), you can file Form 910.00 in it too.
Bank apps — per the KGD, you can file the tax regime notice through them; taxes can be paid, for example, in the Kaspi “Taxes” section.
On paper — at your local tax office (UGD).

In the account, notices and applications go through the “Submit documents” section. Per the KGD, that’s how the notice of the applied tax regime was filed: ISNA account → “Submit documents” → the notice you need → sign with your EDS. Debt and overpayments are shown in your personal account — more on that below.

Your EDS is the key to the account

You sign in and sign documents with your own EDS. It’s issued at pki.gov.kz or a TsON; how to get it and keep it safe is in lesson 2 of the course “IP for a Repair Shop: Open and Run.” For your books one thing matters: anything signed with your EDS counts as done in your name. So never hand the key and password to “helpers,” and take the link to the account from the official kgd.gov.kz website, not from messages or ads.
Personal account: debt or overpayment

Your personal account is a reconciliation with the budget: for each tax you see how much was assessed, how much you paid, and what’s left. What’s left is the balance: zero means all paid, debt means you owe more, overpayment means you paid too much. Per finance.kz (2026), you open it in the ISNA account under “Services” → “Personal account,” and you can generate a statement there too. You can also check for debt with the KGD service “Information on the absence (presence) of debt.”

Per accounting portals, the ISNA system charges penya (late-payment interest) automatically for every day late (how it’s calculated is in lesson 7). The bigger the debt, the tougher the measures. Per mybuh.kz’s breakdown of the new Tax Code (March 18, 2026): a debt of up to 20 MCI (up to ₸86,500 in 2026) gets a debt notice; from 20 to 45 MCI (up to ₸194,625) — a formal notification, suspension of debit transactions on the account, and a collection order; over 45 MCI — an account freeze and an inventory of property. Tax office messages and a zero Form 910.00

Open the tax office messages and notices at least once a month: a notice says what to do and by when (how to reply is in lesson 8). If you don’t file a return on time, the ISNA system files a zero return itself — per the KGD, after that the mistake is fixed with an amended return. Per digitalbusiness.kz (July 30, 2026), you can set up auto-filing of a zero Form 910.00 in the account in advance — that’s for a half-year with no income.

A zero Form 910.00 is only for a half-year with truly no income. A zero return when you had real revenue understates income: you risk an additional tax assessment, penya, and a fine. If it happened, file an amended return with your real income (lesson 8).

How much a simplified-regime IP pays for themselves in 2026 — OPV, OPVR, SO, and VOSMS — what amount they’re based on, how to pay without a code mistake, and how these payments end up on Form 910.00.

Besides the tax every half-year, a simplified-regime IP makes four payments for themselves every month: pension contributions OPV and OPVR, social contributions SO, and health insurance contributions VOSMS. The deadline is the 25th of the following month (lesson 2). Rates and amounts below are for 2026, with a minimum wage of ₸85,000.
Four payments and what they’re based on
OPV — 10% of declared income. The IP declares the income for the math themselves, from 1 to 50× minimum wage a month, so in 2026 the contribution runs from ₸8,500 to ₸425,000.
OPVR — 3.5% of the same declared income (it was 2.5% in 2025): from ₸2,975 to ₸148,750 a month.
SO — 5% of declared income minus OPV; the base is at least 1× and at most 7× minimum wage, so from ₸4,250 to ₸29,750.
VOSMS — 5% of 1.4× minimum wage (₸119,000), so ₸5,950 a month at any income.

A note on sources: the rates for OPV, OPVR, and VOSMS “for yourself” come from the Kaspi Guide and the accounting portal pro1c.kz, and figuring SO on income minus OPV comes from a State Social Insurance Fund (GFSS) clarification (the Social Code itself doesn’t say so directly). Before paying, check the amounts in your bank app or with your local tax office.
