Where to mount the sensor
On a rigid part of the body or a sturdy factory bracket under the dash, close to the middle of the car: that way the sensor hears hits from both sides equally.
Screw the housing down or strap it tight to the bracket. A sensor hanging on its wires sometimes misses a hit and sometimes trips by itself when it swings.
Not on thin plastic and not next to anything that shakes — small motors, the heater blower: the sensor will take their vibration for a hit.
The sensitivity knob should stay reachable for adjustment, but out of sight.
If the shock and tilt sensor is built into the control unit, as in many modern systems, all of these rules apply to where the unit itself goes.

Airbag harnesses run under the dash — they have yellow connectors and often a yellow sleeve. Don’t fasten sensors or their wires to them, don’t splice anything into them, and don’t put sensors where an airbag deploys.
Setting the sensitivity
Start with low sensitivity. The knob is on the sensor housing; built-in sensors are set from the fob, in the app or with software — per your system’s manual.
Arm the car and wait for the sensors to come on: many systems have a delay after arming.
Test it: a light slap with your palm on a body pillar or a tire should give a warning, a harder one an alarm. Don’t hit the glass, and don’t kick the car.
Raise the sensitivity a little at a time and test after every step — on both sides of the car, front and rear.
If the sensor has a separate knob for each zone, the alarm zone must stay noticeably less sensitive than the warning zone.
A good setting: a truck driving past doesn’t trigger an alarm, but the sensor hears a light palm slap.
Tilt and interior motion sensors

The tilt sensor remembers the car’s position when it’s armed and raises the alarm if the position changes: the car is jacked up or loaded onto a tow truck. It ignores slow changes — snow on the roof, tires that have cooled down. It’s mounted rigidly to the body, in the orientation the manual requires.

A microwave interior motion sensor “sees” movement in the cabin and a little around the car — through the glass. It has two zones too: the outer one — someone walked right up — gives a warning, the inner one — a hand inside the cabin — an alarm. It goes near the center of the cabin, for example in the tunnel between the seats, away from metal.

An ultrasonic interior sensor — a transmitter and receiver pair up by the headliner, usually near the dome light — watches the air in the closed cabin. It only works with the windows and sunroof closed.
The motion sensor’s outer zone gives a warning, the inner zone an alarm.

False alarms
Wind and vibration: gusts rock the car, trucks or a streetcar go by, construction is going on nearby. A less sensitive setting helps, especially on tall vehicles and cars with a roof rack.
The sensor is loosely mounted or hangs on its wires — it swings.

A “floating” ground: the sensor or unit ground is on a painted or rusty bolt, or there’s a poor contact in a connector. The unit takes the noise on its input for a trigger. Clean the spot and tighten the ground, as in the lesson on unit power and ground.
A chafed zone wire touches the body — to the unit that’s the same “to ground” signal as the sensor tripping.

For the motion sensor — anything that moves in the closed cabin: a toy or air freshener on the mirror, sunshades, insects, airflow from the heater or a parking heater. For the ultrasonic one — also a window or sunroof left slightly open.
Sometimes false alarms show up only in freezing weather or only in the heat: then recheck the setting in that season.
When to bypass the sensors

Sometimes the car needs to be locked with the sensors bypassed for a while: a dog or cat stays in the cabin, a parking heater or the heater blower is running, the sunroof is open, the car is carried on a tow truck or a ferry. For this, systems let you bypass the sensors or individual zones from the fob or the app — exactly how is in your system’s manual. The pin switches and the engine kill keep working. If the system has remote start, many systems bypass the shock sensor on their own while the engine is running. Explain all this to the customer when you hand the car over.
If the alarm suddenly stops hearing hits or goes completely silent, I check the fuses first — both in the alarm wiring and the factory ones — and only then take panels off and turn knobs.

Siren, antenna and GSM module
Where to put the siren and the fob antenna, why the fob reaches less far than the box says, and what the GSM module needs to stay connected.

The siren, antenna and GSM module are how the alarm talks to the world: the siren to the street, the antenna to the fob, GSM to the owner’s phone. Where they go decides whether the siren is still heard after a few winters, whether the fob reaches the car from the parking lot, and whether alarm messages arrive on time.
Siren: where to mount it
Under the hood, in a protected spot — for example behind the headlight or by the fender, on a sturdy bracket: so the siren is hard to reach from above or below.
Horn facing down: water and dirt drain out instead of collecting inside. A siren with the horn up fills with water, and in winter with ice, and goes quiet.
Away from hot parts — the exhaust manifold, the turbo — and from anything that spins: the radiator fan, belts.

The wire runs in split loom along the factory harnesses and into the cabin through the factory firewall grommet. If you had to drill, fit a rubber grommet and sealant, as in the lesson on routing wires.
The siren ground goes to the body, on a cleaned spot, like the unit ground.

The antenna module — the transceiver — is usually stuck to the inside of the windshield, near the top: from there it “sees” the farthest.
Away from metal — the body frame, metal parts and wiring — at the distance given in the manual. Metal nearby “eats” the range.

Not on metallized tint film and not on an athermal windshield with a coating: the radio signal gets through them poorly. Coated windshields often have an uncoated area, usually by the mirror — check where it is on the actual car.
Not right next to a dash cam or radar detector: their electronics cause interference.
Degrease the glass and stick it on in the warm: tape holds poorly on cold glass. In winter, warm up the cabin first.

Wire routing and installation
How to join wires with solder instead of twisting them, run the harness along the factory one away from moving and hot parts, hide the unit, and reassemble the interior so nothing rattles.

A customer never notices good installation work. Bad work shows up months later: a twisted splice corrodes and the kill relay or central locking fails, a wire chafes through and blows a fuse, the unit knocks under the dash on every bump. The rules in this lesson save you from those comebacks.
Connections: solder, not twists

A twisted splice under tape corrodes over time: resistance grows, the joint heats up, voltage is lost — the lesson on wiring repair covers this in detail. An alarm install has a lot of connections, and each one is soldered or properly crimped. Use neutral flux, such as rosin: acid flux eats copper. Use a soldering iron powerful enough for the solder to flow, not sit in a blob.
Find the wire by measuring, as in the lessons on pin switches and central locking, and check it once more right before you splice in.
Strip a 1–1.5 cm window in the insulation without cutting the strands.
Spread the strands, push the stripped end of the new wire through the gap and wrap it around.
Solder it so the solder flows in between the strands, and let it cool without moving the wire.
Insulate: several layers of tape overlapping the insulation, cloth tape on top. Where heat shrink can be slipped on, use heat shrink.
Strap the tap wire to the factory wire with a zip tie so vibration doesn’t crack the solder joint.
Splicing in without a cut: window, strands, solder, insulation — and the tap wire on a zip tie.

Run the alarm wires along the factory harnesses and zip-tie them at short intervals — the harness must not sag.

Keep clear of everything that moves: pedals, the steering shaft and its U-joint under the dash, seat tracks and mechanisms, door, hood and trunk hinges. Wires go into a door only through the factory boot.

A wire rubbing on the steering shaft, a pedal or a metal edge will sooner or later wear through to the copper. A positive wire on the body is a short circuit: without a fuse it can catch fire, and with a fuse the car is left without the alarm, sometimes without starting. So not a single positive wire without a fuse at the source — as in the lesson on unit power and ground.
The unit: hidden and secure
Hide the control unit deep under the dash and not in the most obvious place: behind the glovebox and under the steering column are where people look first.
The spot must be dry: not on the floor, where meltwater from snowy boots gets in, and not under the windshield, where it may leak.
Zip-tie the unit to a sturdy harness or bracket, and wrap it in cloth tape where it could knock on metal. If the unit has a built-in shock sensor, mount it rigidly, as in the lesson on sensors.
Wrap the wires from the unit the same way as the factory harness next to them — cloth tape or split loom — so they blend in.
Mount the kill relay separately from the unit, somewhere else along the harness, as in the lesson on engine immobilization.
Reassembly order
Reconnect the battery terminal and test all functions while the panels are off: that way a mistake is easy to fix.
Clear the cabin of wire, insulation and zip-tie offcuts.
Plug back in every factory connector you unplugged: switches, lights, sensors.
Refit the panels in reverse order and make sure no wires get caught under clips or screws. Replace broken clips.
Check the factory functions: power windows, lights, the instrument cluster, locks, the horn.
Drive over a rough road and listen: nothing should knock or rattle.

If something rattles after reassembly, look among the things you touched: the unit or a relay touching metal, a loose harness, a panel not fully clipped in. Wrap the unit and relays in cloth tape, zip-tie the harness, replace the clips. In freezing weather plastic is brittle: remove and refit trim in a heated bay, or the clips break and the panels squeak later.

After reassembly I hook up a scan tool and check whether any new codes have appeared in the modules — especially if the alarm is connected over CAN. Go with a Launch scan tool: it’s proven equipment, while cheap ELM327 adapters sometimes “knock the car out”.

Programming and testing
How to learn the fobs and the phone, set the system up for the car and the customer, test every function from a checklist and measure the key-off current with the alarm.

The installation is finished, but don’t put the panels back yet: first the system is programmed and every function is tested — while everything is open, a mistake is easy to fix, as in the lesson on wire routing. Menu names and button sequences differ from system to system, so everything is done per your system’s manual; here is the general order and what gets forgotten most often.

Many systems are set up in the manufacturer’s software on a computer or in the app. For the CAN module you choose the car’s make, model and year there — that decides which commands and statuses it understands, as in the lesson on the CAN bus during installation.
Firmware is updated only with the manufacturer’s official software, and the connection must not be interrupted while writing: a failure halfway through can brick the unit.
When everything is set, save the settings file to the installation archive if the software can do it. If the unit is replaced or reprogrammed, it can be loaded back.
Setting the functions
Central locking pulses — to suit the lock type: positive or negative, duration, double pulse to unlock, as in the lesson on central locking.
Door monitoring delay. If the pin switch wire is taken from the dome light circuit and the light fades out slowly, the system still sees the door as open for a few seconds after it closes.
Passive arming, and automatic rearming if no door is opened after disarming, are handy — but the customer must know about them.
Locking the doors when the ignition is switched on or when driving off, and the chirps when arming and disarming — as the customer prefers.
Sensor sensitivity is set on the spot, as in the lesson on sensors, not left at the factory setting. Write everything you set on the installation card.

Remote start, if the system has it, is only for models the manufacturer supports in its compatibility list: for StarLine it’s can.starline.ru, for Pandora the “Table of commands and statuses” on alarmtrade.ru. It is set up per the manufacturer’s instructions: with an automatic transmission the engine starts only with the selector in P; with a manual, software neutral is needed as well. If the model isn’t on the list, we don’t do remote start, as in the lesson on choosing a system.
Testing from a checklist
Arming: arm and disarm from every fob and from the phone — the siren, turn signals, LED and locks respond as set up.
Doors: arm the system and open each door in turn — an alarm, and on a two-way fob or in the app, the door zone. One door that triggers doesn’t prove the others are connected.
Hood and trunk — separately, each one: an alarm and its own indication.
Sensors: after the delay for them to come on, a light slap on a wheel or pillar gives a warning, a harder one an alarm; tilt and interior sensors too, if fitted.
Central locking: all the doors and the trunk lock and unlock — from the fob and from the phone; the factory button and key work as before.
Turn signals: both sides flash — when arming, disarming and during an alarm.
Engine kill: when armed the engine won’t start; after disarming it starts first time. With the engine running, press the fob buttons and open and close a door — the engine must not stall.
GSM: a command from the phone is carried out and the alarm notification arrives. Remote start, if set up, works only under the conditions the manual allows.

The last measurement is the key-off current: how much the car and the alarm draw from the battery while parked. Measure as in the lesson on parasitic drain: ammeter in the battery negative without breaking the circuit, car locked and armed, hood pin switch held pressed, key well away. Once asleep, a car with an alarm usually draws tens of milliamps; how much the system itself adds is in its manual, and a GSM module adds more than a basic alarm. Write the result on the installation card: if the customer comes back with a flat battery, you’ll have something to compare against.

Handing the car over to the customer
How to teach the customer to use the system, show emergency disarming, do the paperwork and warranty, keep installation photos and be honest about battery drain during long parking.

Handing the car over is part of the installation, not a formality. A customer who didn’t understand how to disarm will call you at night with the siren wailing — and decide the alarm is no good. Allow 15–20 minutes for the handover: at the car, with the customer’s fob and phone in hand. Run through the checklist once more beforehand, as in the lesson on programming and testing: nothing should fail in front of the customer.
Teach them to use it — at the car

A fob can break, get lost or end up with a dead battery. For that there is emergency disarming: with the Valet button and a personal PIN code. On many systems each digit is entered as a number of presses on the button with the ignition on — the exact procedure is in the system’s manual. Show the customer where the button is and let them disarm with the code once themselves. Replace the factory code with a personal one: the customer chooses the digits.

Installation report and warranty card: date, system model and serial number, what was installed — modules, sensors, engine kill — warranty periods for the work and the equipment, signatures. The locations of the unit and the kill relay are not written in the customer’s papers.

Before reassembling the interior, photograph the unit’s location and its connectors, the power, ground, CAN and pin-switch connection points, the kill relay and the alarm fuses. In the same folder goes the installation card with the settings and the key-off current; label the folder with the plate number and the date. A year later the car comes back with a complaint — from the photos you’ll know where everything is within minutes, without stripping half the interior. Keep the photos to yourself and don’t send them to anyone: they’re a map of where the engine kill is.

The alarm keeps working while parked, so it always draws current: together with the car, tens of milliamps, as in the lesson on programming and testing. Do the math with the customer: 40 mA is about 1 Ah a day (0.04 × 24), about 20 Ah in three weeks — a third of a 60 Ah battery. In the cold the battery delivers less, and after a long stand the car may not start even though the alarm is fine.

Faults in an installed alarm
How to track it down when the system won’t arm, gives false alarms, drains the battery, won’t operate the locks, barely hears the fob, or the engine kill stops the car from starting.

Cars with an installed alarm come back with the same complaints over and over. They’re diagnosed like any fault — as in the lesson on the troubleshooting method: ask, confirm, check the simple things, then measure. The photos and installation card from your archive help a lot, as in the lesson on handing the car over: you immediately see where the unit, relay and connection points are. If someone else did the install, start with an inspection: twisted splices, wires without a fuse and connections not done per the manual are obvious right away.

When the alarm is “dead” or one function has gone, I check the fuses first — both the factory ones and the ones in the alarm’s own wiring. Only then do I take off the trim and look at the connections.
Won’t arm

Many systems report which zone is open when you try to arm: with siren chirps or an icon on the fob or in the app — the meanings are in the manual. Most often it’s a pin switch: the system sees a door, the hood or the trunk as open. At the pin-switch input, check with a multimeter or a logic probe whether the signal changes as you open and close, as in the lesson on pin switches. Causes: a corroded or stuck pin switch, a hood switch knocked out of place after a repair, a chafed wire touching the body, water in a connector, a dome light with a fade-out delay. If the system doesn’t respond at all — the fob battery, then the unit’s power and ground.
Example — a ground-side pin switch: the door is closed, yet the input reads 0 V — the unit treats it as open.
Pin switch
input
Door open — 0 V at the input
Door closed — 12 V: the unit sees “closed”

Door closed, yet 0 V at the input — the unit sees “open”
Start with the alarm memory: the system remembers which zone triggered — on the fob, in the app or by LED flashes. Without it you’re searching blind.
Shock or tilt sensor: sensitivity set too high, the sensor poorly mounted, wind and passing trucks — the settings and the location, as in the lesson on sensors.
Interior sensor: a window or sunroof left ajar, things swinging in the cabin, airflow from the heater.
Doors, hood, trunk: a pin switch with a poor contact or a chafed wire sets off the alarm when the wind rocks the car. The hood switch suffers from dirt and water more than the others.

A poor ground or power feed to the unit: the voltage “wanders” and the unit takes noise for a trigger. The drop on the ground and on the positive is checked with the siren on, as in the lesson on the unit’s power and ground.
Drains the battery
Check the battery itself: charge and condition. An old battery may simply not hold a charge.
Measure the key-off current after the modules fall asleep, as in the lesson on parasitic drain, and compare it with the reading on the installation card.
If the current is higher, find out how much of it the alarm takes: from the voltage drop across its fuse, without pulling it.

The alarm draws a lot: with weak coverage the GSM module keeps searching for the network; the unit can’t sleep because it sees an open door; the kill relay coil is energized for the whole time the car is parked — that’s about 0.1–0.15 A.
The alarm is fine but the car won’t go to sleep — check the CAN module settings: a wrongly configured module can keep the modules awake. After that, hunt for the drain by the usual method.
Central locking doesn’t work

Doesn’t work from the fob but works from the factory button — look in the installation: the fuse and power for the lock outputs, the pulse type, its duration, the contact at the connection point, as in the lesson on central locking.

Doesn’t work from the factory button either: on reversing actuators the wires are cut and routed through the relays’ normally closed contacts. If such a contact corrodes, the locks won’t work from anything — yet the installation is to blame.
Works only sometimes, worse in the cold — the pulse is too short for the actuator or the actuator itself is weak: lengthen the pulse per the manual and check the actuator.
Control over CAN — check the CAN module settings and its connection to the pair, as in the lesson on the CAN bus during installation.
Poor fob range
The fob battery comes first and is the most common cause. Compare with the second fob: if that one reaches farther, the problem is in the first fob.

The antenna: it came unstuck, was moved, its wire got pinched during reassembly, there’s metal nearby or metallized tint — range often drops after tinting, as in the lesson on the siren, antenna and GSM.
Interference: downtown, in a big parking lot, near power lines the range is lower for every system. Check somewhere else — if it’s fine there, it isn’t a fault.
Won’t start because of the engine kill

First make sure the system is disarmed and that the kill isn’t switched on by design — for example, a mode where starting needs a tag or a code — per the manual. Then measure with the ignition on while the pump primes, or while cranking: the voltage before and after the kill relay contact. The same on both sides — the relay isn’t to blame; keep going along the circuit. Voltage before the contact but none after — the relay isn’t passing it: on a normally closed relay the contact is burnt or the coil is getting a signal even though the alarm is disarmed; on a normally open relay the coil isn’t getting its signal. Contacts burn when the relay was chosen without a current margin, as in the lesson on the engine kill. Re-solder any corroded twisted splice in the circuit.

Won’t arm — most often a pin switch: with the door closed, the input must read “closed”.
Drains the battery — key-off current against the handover reading and the drop across the alarm fuse; common culprits are GSM, a unit that won’t sleep, an energized relay coil.

Starting a diesel in winter
How glow plugs and preheating work, why fuel matters in winter, and what to do if your diesel won’t start in the cold.

A diesel has no spark plugs: the fuel ignites on its own from the strong compression of hot air. In freezing weather the cold metal soaks up the heat, and without help the engine won’t catch. Three things help: glow plugs, preheating and the right fuel.
Glow plugs

These are electric heaters in each cylinder. When you switch on the ignition, a relay or a glow plug control unit powers them, and a yellow coil symbol lights up on the dashboard. While it’s on, the plugs are heating the combustion chambers.
Switch on the ignition and don’t touch the starter until the coil symbol goes out.
Switch off the headlights, the heater and any seat or window heating; with a manual transmission, press the clutch.
Start the engine. If it doesn’t catch, switch off the ignition and heat the glow plugs again.
On many cars the glow plugs keep working after the engine starts, until it warms up: that way it runs more smoothly and smokes less.

Signs of faulty glow plugs: in the cold the starter cranks briskly, but the engine is slow to catch, runs rough for the first few minutes and puts out thick white smoke. On many cars a coil symbol flashing while you drive signals a fault — read the codes. A mechanic will check the glow plugs and the glow plug relay with a multimeter or a clamp meter.
Check the fuses first. If the coil symbol doesn’t light up or the plugs clearly aren’t heating, start by checking the high-current fuse and the glow plug relay.

Many truck diesels — KamAZ, Shacman, Howo — have no glow plugs in the cylinders: in winter an air heater in the intake manifold does the job, either an electric grid heater or a flame-start unit. The procedure is the same: wait for the ready signal on the dashboard.
Engine preheating
A plug-in electric heater running on 220 V mains warms the coolant; it’s usually switched on 1–2 hours before you set off.
A coolant parking heater (Webasto Thermo Top, Eberspächer Hydronic, Binar) warms the engine and the cabin using fuel from the tank, on a timer or from a remote. More on this in the next lesson.
A fuel filter heater keeps the diesel from thickening at the narrowest point.

The extension cord for a 220 V heater must be in good condition, rated for outdoor use, grounded and rated for the heater’s power. Keep the connections dry. Insulation that has cracked in the cold is an electric shock risk.
Winter fuel

Summer diesel turns cloudy in the cold: wax (paraffin) crystals form in it. They clog the fuel filter, and the engine is starved of fuel. Diesel fuel comes in summer (L), off-season (E), winter (Z) and arctic (A) grades. For freezing weather you need winter or arctic fuel — fill up with it at trusted gas stations in advance, before the cold sets in.
Anti-gel (a cold-flow additive) is added before the frost, while the fuel is still clear. It won’t dissolve wax that has already formed.
Don’t dilute diesel with gasoline: it harms modern diesels — the high-pressure fuel pump and the injectors suffer.
Before winter, replace the filter if it’s due, and drain off the water that has settled in it if the filter has a drain valve.
Won’t start in the cold — what to do
The starter cranks sluggishly — it’s the battery: charge it or jump-start it properly, as in the battery lesson.
It cranks briskly but doesn’t catch, and there’s white smoke — suspect the glow plugs: heat them again, then see a mechanic.
After a freezing night it catches and stalls, or doesn’t catch at all — the fuel has probably gelled. Tow the car into a heated garage for a few hours until the wax melts, then replace the filter.
Crank the starter for no more than 10 seconds at a time, with pauses, or you’ll drain the battery.

Don’t heat the filter, fuel lines or tank with an open flame — a blowtorch, a torch or a bonfire: there’s fuel and wiring nearby. Don’t use “quick start” spray unless the owner’s manual allows it: with glow plugs or an intake air heater, the mixture can ignite in the intake and damage the engine.
A diesel starts from compression; in the cold, glow plugs or an intake air heater help it.
Start the engine after the coil symbol goes out; if it doesn’t catch, heat the plugs again.
In winter, use winter or arctic fuel; anti-gel goes in before the frost.
Cranks briskly but won’t catch — glow plugs; catches and stalls after a freezing night — fuel.
No open flames near the fuel system: wax is melted in a heated garage.
In freezing weather, when can you crank the starter on a diesel?
Right after turning the key
After the coil symbol on the dashboard goes out
Only 5 minutes after switching on the ignition
While the coil symbol is on, the glow plugs are heating the combustion chambers. You crank the starter once it goes out; if the engine doesn’t catch, you repeat the preheating.
The starter cranks briskly, the engine won’t catch, and thick white smoke comes out of the exhaust. What does this point to?
A faulty starter
The glow plugs aren’t heating
Brisk cranking means the battery and the starter are fine. White smoke and poor starting in the cold are a typical sign of faulty glow plugs.
When does anti-gel help?
If you add it before the frost, while the fuel is clear
If you add it to fuel that has already gelled
If you pour it into the washer fluid reservoir
The additive stops wax from forming, but it doesn’t dissolve crystals that have already formed. That’s why it’s added in advance.
After a freezing night, wax has formed in the diesel fuel and the engine won’t start. What’s the right thing to do?
Warm the filter with a blowtorch
Dilute the fuel with gasoline
Keep cranking until it starts
Tow the car into a heated garage, then replace the filter
In the warmth the wax will melt on its own. An open flame near the fuel system can end in a fire, and gasoline damages a diesel’s fuel injection system.
Parking heater: using it without mistakes
How to switch a parking heater on and off properly, why it goes into a fault, and what you can check yourself before heading to a mechanic.

A parking heater produces heat without the engine running: it burns fuel from the tank in its own combustion chamber. Air heaters — Planar, Webasto Air Top, Eberspächer Airtronic, Chinese “diesel air heaters” — warm the car interior or the truck cab. Coolant heaters — Webasto Thermo Top, Eberspächer Hydronic, Binar — warm the coolant, and with it the engine and the cabin heater.
How it works

A metering pump feeds small amounts of fuel into the chamber, a glow plug ignites it, a fan blows in air for combustion, and the exhaust goes outside through its own pipe. The control unit monitors the flame, temperature and voltage. If something is wrong, it shuts the heater down and shows a fault code.
How to use it
Switch it on with the control panel, the timer or the remote. Ignition takes a few minutes — that’s normal.

Switch it off only with the button. After that, the heater purges and cools down for a few minutes. While it’s purging, don’t disconnect the battery terminal or turn off the battery master switch on a truck — that’s how parking heaters get overheated and ruined.
Frequent short runs do harm: the chamber doesn’t have time to heat up, and carbon builds up.
In summer, run the heater once a month for about 10 minutes so the pump and the fan don’t seize up.
Turn the heater off at gas stations.

A parking heater’s exhaust is carbon monoxide. Don’t run it in a closed garage, and make sure the exhaust pipe is intact and vents outside. Exhaust smell in the cabin, a headache, drowsiness — switch it off at once, air out the car and see a mechanic. Cheap “diesel air heaters” installed carelessly are especially prone to this.
It’s showing a fault — what to check yourself
Most faults aren’t a breakdown of the heater itself — they come down to power, fuel or air. Check in this order:

Voltage. During ignition the glow plug draws a lot of current, and a weak battery dips below the protection threshold. At rest the battery should read 12,4–12,9 V; on a truck with a 24 V system, twice that — 24,8–25,8 V. Check the terminals too: a corroded contact has the same effect.

Fuel. The heater’s fuel pickup often sits higher than the engine’s, and when the tank is nearly empty the heater can no longer reach the fuel. In winter, keep the tank at least a quarter full. Summer diesel gels first in the heater’s thin fuel line — you need winter fuel, as in the lesson on winter starting.
Air intake and exhaust. Their pipes are outside, under the floor or by the frame: snow, ice and dirt clog them, and a crushed pipe chokes the combustion. Clean and inspect them.
On an air heater — the warm air outlet. A bag or a jacket over the grille, and it goes into an overheating fault.
Check the fuses first. A parking heater usually has its own fuse, often a separate one on the power wire near the battery.

The control panel shows the fault code — as a number on the display or as a number of flashes of the indicator. To find out what it means for your model, see the “Error codes” tab, in the parking heaters section.

After several failed starts in a row, or after overheating, many heaters lock out. The lockout is cleared following the manual or by a mechanic with diagnostic equipment. Don’t keep switching the heater on again and again “just in case it works”: unburned fuel builds up in the chamber.
When to see a mechanic
The fault keeps coming back even though the voltage, fuel and pipes are fine.
Codes for the glow plug, flame sensor, pump, fan or overheating.
Exhaust or fuel smell in the cabin, smoke from under the car, fuel leaks.
The heater is locked out.
Switch it off only with the button; don’t cut the purge short by disconnecting the battery terminal or the master switch.
A common cause of faults is a weak battery: at rest 12,4–12,9 V, on a 24-volt vehicle 24,8–25,8 V.
In winter, keep the tank at least a quarter full, with winter fuel.
The air intake and exhaust are clean and intact; the exhaust vents only outside.
Codes are on the “Error codes” tab; if the fault returns after these checks, or there’s an exhaust smell or a lockout — see a mechanic.
What’s the right way to switch off a parking heater?
Turn off the battery master switch right away so the battery doesn’t drain
With the button on the control panel, then wait for the purge to finish
Disconnect the battery terminal
After you switch it off, the heater purges and cools the chamber. If you cut the power before that, it will overheat and may fail.
In winter the parking heater won’t start, and the tank is almost empty. What’s the most likely cause?
The control unit has burned out
The alternator is faulty
The heater needs to be switched on more often
The heater’s fuel pickup is higher, and it can’t reach the fuel
The heater’s fuel line often draws fuel from higher up than the engine’s pump. With the tank nearly empty, the engine still runs, but the parking heater is already out of fuel.
The heater goes into a voltage fault. What should you check first?
The battery charge and the condition of the terminals
The engine oil level
Tire pressure
During ignition the heater’s glow plug draws a lot of current. A weak battery or a poor contact at the terminal makes the voltage dip below the protection threshold.
While the parking heater is running, there’s an exhaust smell in the cabin. What should you do?
Open a window a little and ignore it
Turn the heater up to full power
Switch it off, air out the car and go to a mechanic
An exhaust smell means carbon monoxide may be getting into the cabin. It has no color and can poison you without you noticing.
Car alarm and remote start
Why a car alarm can drain the battery and stop the key fob from working, how to unlock and start the car with the key, and when you need an installer.

A car alarm with remote start is very handy in winter. But it comes with common complaints: the battery has died, the fob doesn’t respond, the car won’t unlock. You can sort out most of these cases yourself.
Why the battery drains

Remote start on a timer or by temperature, without any driving. Starting in the cold takes a lot of energy from the battery, and 10–20 minutes at idle puts little back. A few days of warm-ups like this, and the battery is dead.
The alarm itself. It draws current all the time, and GSM and GPS modules draw noticeably more. Over a week or two of the car sitting, it adds up.

An installation mistake: the alarm keeps the car’s control units from “going to sleep”, or powers something constantly where it should be powered from the ignition. A parasitic draw test will show it, as in the multimeter lesson.

What helps: drive regularly, at least half an hour at a time, top up the battery with a charger from time to time, and don’t set remote start too often. Many alarms have a low-battery-voltage start feature — it keeps the battery from going completely flat.
The key fob doesn’t work
The fob doesn’t respond or only works up close — first check the fob battery. In the cold, a weak battery gives out faster. Its type is marked inside the fob or in the manual.
The fob works, but the car doesn’t respond and the interior lights don’t come on — the car battery is dead.
The fob has poor range in just one spot — that’s radio interference; move closer.
The fob has “lost” the car after a battery change or a knock — it needs to be paired again following the alarm manual; sometimes only an installer can do this.
How to unlock and start with the key
Take out the mechanical key: on most key fobs it slides out or can be pulled out of the housing.
Unlock the driver’s door. The lock cylinder is sometimes hidden under a cap on the handle — the owner’s manual explains how to remove it.
If the siren goes off, disarm the alarm with the fob or with the emergency override — the Valet button and your PIN code, following the alarm manual.
If the battery is dead, open the hood with the lever inside the car and charge or jump-start the battery, as in the battery lesson.
On a push-button start car with a dead key fob, hold the key against the button or the spot shown in the owner’s manual.
Keep the alarm manual, the spare fob and your PIN code at home, not in the car. When buying a car with an alarm, get all the fobs, the manual and the code from the previous owner.

If the hood has an electric lock, it won’t open when the battery is dead. Ask the installer in advance how to supply power in that case. Don’t cut or bridge the alarm wires to start the car: the immobilizer is designed precisely against that, and repairing the wiring will cost more than calling out the installer.
Check the fuses first. If the alarm shows no signs of life even though the battery is charged, check its own fuse on the power wire.
When you need an installer
The battery started draining after the alarm was installed.
False alarms from wind and passing cars — the shock sensor needs adjusting.
Remote start doesn’t work, or the engine stalls right after it.
After installation, warning lights came on on the dashboard or factory features stopped working.
You need to pair a new key fob.
Remote start without driving drains the battery: starting takes more than warming up gives back.
The fob doesn’t respond — check its battery first; the car doesn’t respond at all — the car battery is dead.
The mechanical key is hidden in the fob; the siren is turned off with the fob or the Valet code, following the manual.
Keep the manual, the code and the spare fob at home.
Parasitic draw after installation, false alarms, remote start failures — see the installer.
For a week the car warmed up on a remote start timer but never went anywhere, and the battery died. Why?
Starting takes more energy than warming up at idle gives back
The key fob broke
That can’t happen — only the alternator is to blame
Starting in the cold drains the battery a lot, and a short run at idle doesn’t have time to make up for it. You need to drive or recharge the battery.
The fob no longer unlocks the car, but when you unlock it with the key, the interior lights come on and everything works. What should you check first?
The key fob battery
The headlight fuse
If the car is alive, the battery is fine. Most often the culprit is a dead fob battery, especially in the cold.
How do you get into the car if the battery is dead?
Break a window
Wait for the battery to recover on its own
Unlock the driver’s door with the mechanical key from the fob
Almost every key fob has a mechanical key. After that, the siren is turned off with the fob or the Valet code, following the manual.
After an alarm was installed, the battery goes flat after a few days of sitting. What should you do?
Fit a bigger battery
Cut the alarm wire
Nothing — that’s how it’s supposed to be
