Hybrids and electric vehicles: what a scan tool shows

What a scan tool can read on a hybrid or electric vehicle — the state of charge, battery voltages and temperatures, BMS codes, insulation monitoring — why the car often “won’t switch on” because of the 12-volt battery, and how frosts affect the battery.

Hybrids and electric vehicles are scanned in the same order: all modules, codes, freeze frames, live data. What’s new is the BMS, the battery management module: it monitors the traction battery’s voltage, current and temperature. What’s under high voltage in such a car and what an auto electrician may do without certification is covered in the lesson on hybrids and electric vehicles in the auto electrician course. Here — what you see on the screen and how to read it.

Orange wires and connectors are high voltage, deadly even when the car is switched off. Don’t touch or disconnect them. Work on the high-voltage system and its service functions in the scan tool — tests, relearning, preparing the battery for removal — is done only by trained, certified specialists. Without certification, the scan tool is only for reading codes and data. In READY mode the car sits silently, but a hybrid’s engine can start by itself: before working under the hood, switch the system off and take the key away.
“Won’t switch on” — check the 12-volt battery first

The traction battery doesn’t start the system by itself. The control modules and the relays that connect the high-voltage battery are powered from the ordinary 12-volt system. If the small 12-volt battery is flat, the car won’t go into READY, the dash flickers or goes dark, and the scan tool finds communication and low-voltage faults in many modules at once. That’s the result of one cause, not a dozen failures — as in the lesson on fault codes.
Check the 12-volt battery voltage at rest and while trying to switch to READY — as in the lesson on the battery.
Charge it in the mode for its type, often AGM; connect jumper cables only to the points shown in the manual.
While you scan with READY off, keep the 12-volt system on a battery maintainer: the small battery drains quickly.
Record the codes, charge the battery, clear the low-voltage faults and read all the modules again. Whatever remains — work through it in order.
Check the fuses first. If a hybrid won’t wake up even with a charged 12-volt battery, check the 12-volt system fuses before thinking about an expensive repair.
What the BMS shows

SOC — the state of charge as a percentage. A hybrid that doesn’t plug into an outlet keeps it in the middle range: it never fully charges the battery or runs it down to zero — that’s normal. On an electric vehicle, the percentage in the module and on the dash may not match: the manufacturer keeps a reserve.
SOH — an estimate of battery wear. Not every car and not every scan tool has it.
Cell or module voltages. The battery is made up of many cells, and their groups are called modules or blocks. The BMS measures each group, and the scan tool shows a list, the minimum and the maximum.
Temperatures from several battery sensors, the battery current, the cooling fan or pump operation.
BMS codes — record them together with the freeze frame, like any others.
Insulation — the module constantly checks for leakage from the high-voltage circuit to the body.
Voltage spread

With the voltages, the key thing isn’t a single number but the spread: the difference between the highest and the lowest module. In a healthy battery the modules are close to each other. A weak module gives itself away under load and at a low state of charge: on acceleration all the voltages sag a little, but its voltage sags noticeably more. So look both at rest and while driving, or better still, record a graph of the drive, as in the lesson on graphs and recording; on the road, a helper watches the scan tool. The allowable spread is in the manufacturer’s data. The generic code P0A80 — “replace hybrid battery pack” — is often linked to exactly this spread between modules. Whether to repair the modules or replace the battery is decided by a certified specialist after testing.
Temperatures and insulation

The temperature sensors are located in different parts of the battery. A large difference between them or fast heating during gentle driving is a reason to check the cooling. On many hybrids the battery is cooled by a fan using air from the cabin, and an intake grille clogged with dust is a common cause of overheating. The grille in the cabin is cleaned as the manual describes; everything behind the battery covers is a job for a certified specialist. Electric vehicles more often have liquid cooling — check the scan tool data and the manual.

The high-voltage circuit isn’t connected to the body. The module constantly checks the insulation resistance between them. If it drops, the module stores a code, and the system may not go into READY or may disconnect the battery. Causes — moisture, a damaged cable, the wrong oil in the electric A/C compressor, as in the lesson on hybrids. The scan tool will show the code and sometimes the insulation value. Measuring insulation with a megohmmeter and looking for the leak — only for a certified specialist.
Winter: frost and charging

In our frosts, a lithium battery delivers less energy and accepts charge less well. While it’s cold, the module limits the charging power, so in winter charging, especially fast charging, takes longer. In live data you can see this from the battery temperature and the charging current.
The range is noticeably shorter in winter: energy also goes into heating the cabin and the battery. In frost a hybrid starts its engine more often to warm up and heat the cabin — that’s normal.
Charge right after a drive, while the battery is warm. If the car can heat the battery and the cabin from the grid, turn on preheating while it’s charging.
Don’t leave the car out in the frost for a long time with an almost empty battery.
Charge from a working outlet and a cable rated for that current, without thin extension cords. Clear snow and ice from the charging port carefully, and don’t yank a frozen-in connector out by force.
The 12-volt battery suffers from the cold just like in an ordinary car — check it before winter.
We don’t touch orange wires; high-voltage work and service functions — only a certified specialist; without certification, the scan tool is for reading only.
“Won’t switch on” — first the 12-volt battery and its fuses: this system is what wakes up the traction battery’s modules and relays.
In the BMS, look at the SOC, the module voltage spread at rest and under load, temperatures, codes and insulation.
In winter the battery charges more slowly: charge right after a drive, preheat from the grid, don’t leave it discharged in the frost.
A hybrid won’t go into READY, the dash flickers, and a dozen modules have communication and low-voltage faults. Where do you start?
Replace the traction battery

Remove the service disconnect plug
The traction battery’s modules and relays are powered from the 12-volt system. Low voltage causes faults in many modules at once.

In winter, an electric vehicle takes noticeably longer to charge than in summer. Why?
While the battery is cold, the module limits the charging power
The charging port is faulty
Frost damages the charging cable

A cold lithium battery accepts charge poorly, and the module protects it. As it warms up, the charging power increases.
Customer report and working with information

How to save a scan tool report with codes, freeze frames and before-and-after graphs, explain to the customer in simple words what’s urgent and what can wait, back up your findings, where to get verified data and how to keep your own case database.

Diagnostics is finished when the customer understands what was found and what to do about it, and you have records you can show today and find a year from now. General rules for reports and warranties are in the lesson on the auto electrician profession. Here — how to do it with a scan tool.
Saving the scan tool report
Codes from all modules — before clearing, as in the lesson on the diagnostic procedure. Freeze frames separately: they show the conditions under which the fault appeared.
Identification: VIN, mileage, module and software numbers — the scan tool usually puts them at the top of the report.
Graphs and live data recordings — as a file, if the scan tool can do that. If not — a screenshot or a photo where the parameter name, the numbers and the units are visible.
Many scan tools have a report function: save to a file or PDF. In the file name — the date, the make, the license plate or the last digits of the VIN, “before” or “after”.
Keep it in two places — on your phone or laptop and in the cloud. You can send the report to the customer on WhatsApp or by email.

Before and after. Record the same parameters under the same conditions — warm idle, 2500 rpm, a test drive — before the repair and after it. How to record and choose the parameters is in the lesson on graphs and recording. Two graphs side by side are more convincing than any words: the customer sees what they’re paying for, and you see that the repair really helped.
Explaining in simple words
Start with the main thing: what’s wrong, what it could lead to, what you suggest and how much it costs.

No jargon. Not “P0171, long-term trim plus twenty”, but “the engine is sucking in extra air, and the module adds fuel to make up for it — that’s where the rough idle and the fuel consumption come from”.
Show them: the scan tool screen, a graph, a photo of the faulty spot.
Separate what’s confirmed from what’s assumed. A code isn’t a verdict on a part: until a measurement has confirmed it, say “I suspect this circuit, I’ll check it with a measurement”.
Don’t scare the customer and don’t promise too much. There may be several causes — say what you’ll check first and why.
What’s urgent and what can wait

Sort your findings into three groups, like a traffic light. Urgent — anything that makes driving dangerous or could damage the engine: brakes, airbags, steering, overheating, low oil pressure — as in the lesson on dashboard warning lights — and a flashing check engine light: it usually means severe misfires that ruin the catalytic converter. Soon — things that still work but will let you down: a weak battery before winter, an air leak with a positive fuel trim. Can wait — things that don’t affect safety or the engine: an interior light that doesn’t work, or the module has found a leak in the fuel vapor system — often it’s just a loosely closed fuel cap. The customer decides, but the choice must be an informed one.

If a fault threatens safety — brakes, airbags, steering — say so directly and note on the work order that the customer has been warned. If they decline the repair, write that down too. On a test drive, a helper watches the scan tool or the scan tool records the data: the driver watches the road.
Photos and video as evidence
At check-in — the dash with the warning lights on and the mileage, with the customer present.
The scan tool screen with the codes and values — close up, so the numbers can be read.
A measurement: both the probes at the measuring point and the multimeter or oscilloscope reading in the frame.
The faulty spot before and after: a corroded connector, a chafed wire, a melted fuse socket. Give the old parts to the customer.
Video — for what a photo can’t show: an intermittent fault, a sound, flickering lights, an actuator working during a test.
Photos of a customer’s car on social media — only with their consent and without the license plate and VIN.
Where to get data

Take wiring diagrams, pinouts, specs and service procedures from verified sources: Autodata, HaynesPro, the manufacturer’s official documentation — repair manuals and service bulletins. They cost money, but a mistake made from a random diagram costs more. Forums and videos are useful as a hint on where to look, but not as a spec: they often mix up engines, years and markets — the wiring on a right-hand-drive Japanese car and on the same model for a different market can differ. Verify any forum advice with a wiring diagram and a measurement.
Your own case database
A spreadsheet or notes on your phone are enough — the main thing is to have the same fields in every entry. Keep the VIN and the customer’s contact details only for yourself.
The car: make, model, engine, year, market — for example, a right-hand-drive Japanese car.
The complaint in the customer’s words and the conditions: cold or hot engine, frost, rain, bumps.
Codes and freeze frames — as the report file; key measurements — with the numbers and the measuring point.
The cause and exactly where it was: a connector, a section of the harness, a part. What helped and what didn’t — the second saves as much time as the first.
How long the job took — so you can quote times and prices honestly.
Search tags: make, code, system, symptom. And record the values from healthy cars — you’ll have something to compare with.
Scan tool report: codes from all modules before clearing, freeze frames, identification, and before-and-after graphs under the same conditions; keep it in two places.
For the customer — in simple words and by the traffic light: urgent, soon, can wait; keep what’s confirmed separate from assumptions.
Photos and video: the dash at check-in, the scan tool screen, a measurement with its reading, the faulty spot before and after.
Data — from Autodata, HaynesPro and the manufacturer’s documentation; a forum is only a hint that you verify with a measurement; your own cases go into a database with tags.

Connecting a module on the bench without a diagram

How to find the grounds, power feeds, +15, main relay control and the diagnostic line from the board and a multimeter when there’s no pinout, power such a module up safely for the first time and record what you found for the future.

A module’s pinout is taken from verified sources, as in the lesson on connecting on the bench. But sometimes it can’t be found anywhere: a rare model, a Chinese car or special equipment, an old right-hand-drive Japanese car. Then the pins are identified from the board itself and a multimeter. It takes longer, but the board gives away a lot by itself: wide traces, familiar parts, telltale readings in diode test mode.
Inspection first
Photograph both sides of the board and the connector — close up, in good light: on a photo it’s easy to follow traces and label what you find.

Find the familiar sections, as in the lesson on what’s inside an ECU: the regulator, the large electrolytics at the power input, the drivers on the heat sink, the transceiver near the connector, the processor.
Look at trace widths. Power, grounds and outputs to heavy loads run on wide traces, often through several neighboring pins; sensor and bus signals run on thin ones.
All measurements before the first power-up are made on an unpowered module with the connector unplugged.
Grounds

Put one probe on board ground: a large copper pour, the negative of a big electrolytic, the regulator’s heat-sink tab — on many regulators it’s connected to ground. If these points read a dead short to each other, that’s definitely ground. Run the other probe across every connector pin. Ground reads almost a dead short — a fraction of an ohm, and the meter beeps. There are usually several such pins: power grounds on wide traces, sensor grounds on thin ones. A few ohms or more is no longer ground but a circuit through a resistor or a part.
Probing against ground in diode test mode

Multimeter in diode test mode, as in the lesson on board components. Black probe on ground, red on each connector pin in turn. Then the other way round: red on ground, black across the pins. Write down two readings for each pin. There’s no second module to compare against here, so look at the circuit’s “signature”: the pair of readings hints at what sits behind the pin.
Two readings — one in each direction — hint at what sits behind the pin.

Almost 0 in both directions — ground.
Red on the pin — the reading climbs and goes to OL: the meter is charging a big capacitor through a protection diode. That’s how power inputs look — +30 and the feed from the main relay.

Red on the pin — OL, black on the pin — about 0.5 V: that’s a MOSFET’s body diode, a low-side driver output. Several pins with identical readings are a group of identical outputs: injectors, coils, valves.
Sensor and bus inputs go through resistors and protection diodes, so their readings are higher and vary. Diode mode alone won’t identify such a pin — the trace helps from here.

When there’s no diagram, I first find ground by probing, then, relative to it, I look in diode test mode for the positive that should be on the pins, and work my way through the rest of them. That way you can connect a module on the bench even without a ready-made diagram.
Where the trace leads

+30, constant positive, is a wide trace through a reverse-polarity diode to a large electrolytic and the regulator input; a suppressor — a diode that absorbs spikes — often sits nearby. The feed from the main relay takes a similar path, often through two or three neighboring pins.
+15, ignition, is a thin trace through a resistor or resistor divider to the processor, and often to the power supply chip as well: this is the signal that wakes the module up.
Main relay control is a low-side transistor output. Its readings look just like the driver outputs, so the first power-up will show which output is the relay.

CAN-H and CAN-L are a pair of thin traces running side by side to the transceiver — an 8-pin chip near the connector, often through a small choke. There’s about 120 Ω between the pins if the module has a termination resistor (sometimes it’s two 60 Ω resistors with a capacitor in the middle — the same 120 in total); without one, the resistance is high. You see 60 Ω on a car, where the bus has two 120 Ω resistors.
K-line is a single thin pin going to its own transistor or a small transceiver chip.
Outputs to injectors, coils and valves are wide traces to the drivers and switching transistors on the heat sink.
Each circuit is recognized by the part the trace from the pin leads to.

Don’t apply positive to a pin whose function hasn’t been confirmed by both the readings and the trace. It’s especially dangerous to mistake the 5 V sensor reference output for a power input: in diode mode it “charges up” too, but its trace comes from the regulator output instead of going to its input. 12 V on that pin can burn out the regulator and the processor. Don’t put any load on direct-injection or Common Rail injector outputs on the bench: they carry tens to hundreds of volts.
First power-up

Power supply at 13.5 V, current limit 0.3–0.5 A — lower than usual: if there’s a mistake in your table, the current will hit the limit before anything burns. If you don’t know whether the module is 12 V or 24 V, start at 12 V: too low a voltage just won’t wake it up, while too high can burn it out.
Power supply output off. Negative to all the grounds you found, positive through a fuse to the +30 you found, and to the +15 pin through a switch. Leave the other pins free for now.

Switch the output on: the current is almost zero, a few milliamps — the module is asleep. If the current is at the limit right away, switch off: there’s a mistake in the table or a short in the module.
Switch on +15: the current steps up to tens or hundreds of milliamps and holds steady — the module has woken up, as in the lesson on connecting on the bench.

For the first few minutes, watch the ammeter and the board. If the current creeps up or hits the limit, or there’s a smell, crackling or a part heating up — switch off at once and look for the mistake.

The module is alive: relay and communication

Main relay. Connect LEDs with a resistor of about 1 kΩ from positive to the pins with a driver-output “signature”, as in the lesson on output stages. The relay output switches on right after +15 and stays on, and after +15 is switched off it doesn’t go out at once. One that lights for a couple of seconds and goes out is more likely the fuel pump relay. The bench relay gives the final confirmation: a click — and the “power from relay” pins receive positive.

Communication. CAN-H and CAN-L to pins 6 and 14 of the OBD-II connector, K-line to pin 7, the adapter powered from the same supply, and a 120 Ω resistor if the module has none of its own — as in the lesson on connecting on the bench. Swapped CAN-H and CAN-L won’t damage the transceiver: there just won’t be any communication — swap them back. Some modules have two CAN pairs, and diagnostics may be on only one of them.

Read the identification data — module number, software number and version — and check it against the label. No communication — check the 5 V at the regulator output and the crystal, as in the lesson on a module that won’t communicate.

A burnt-out driver: building a replacement from transistors
How a multi-channel driver is built, when a burnt-out channel can be replaced with a MOSFET circuit and when it can’t, and how to build, fit and test such a channel.

The right way to replace a burnt-out driver is with an identical chip, as in the lesson on output stages. But it may not be in stock, and an order takes weeks. That’s where it helps that a multi-channel driver is essentially several switching transistors in one package. A burnt-out channel can be built from a separate transistor and a few small parts. It isn’t “factory original”, but in the right cases it’s a working repair.
What’s inside a multi-channel driver

A multi-channel driver is a chip with several switches. Usually they’re low-side switches: each one switches its load’s negative to ground, as in the lesson on actuators. Besides the switches, there’s protection inside — against shorts, overheating and the spike when a coil turns off — and diagnostics: the chip itself detects an open or shorted load and reports it to the processor. That’s where “open circuit” and “short to positive” codes come from.
With parallel inputs: each channel has its own IN input, and the processor switches the channel on with a voltage on it. The signal can be seen with an oscilloscope right at the driver input.
Controlled over SPI, a serial bus: the processor sends commands as digital code for all channels at once. There’s no separate switch-on signal for a channel on the board.
Mixed: some channels are switched by IN inputs, some only over SPI, and the chip reports diagnostics over SPI.
One package holds several switches with shared protection and diagnostics.

When a transistor replacement is possible
A channel with a parallel input: on a running module, the oscilloscope shows pulses from the processor at the burnt-out channel’s input.
The load is a relay, valve, lamp or a high-impedance injector of about 12–16 Ω that the driver simply switches on and off.

Low-impedance injectors, usually about 2–3 Ω, are driven by some modules with current control — “peak and hold”: a high current first to open, then a lower one to hold. A simple switch can’t replace such a channel. Check the chip’s datasheet to see how your channel works.

Don’t attempt this replacement if the channel is controlled only over SPI: there’s nothing to take the signal from. Don’t replace ignition drivers this way: ignition transistors (IGBTs) work with spikes of hundreds of volts and current limiting, and a plain MOSFET can’t replace them. Direct-injection and Common Rail injector outputs, H-bridge motor drivers and high-side switches are out too. And never in safety systems: airbags, ABS, electric power steering. There it’s only the original part or a replacement module.
One channel’s circuit

The transistor is a logic-level N-channel MOSFET: it turns fully on from logic voltage. Its on-resistance must be specified at a gate voltage no higher than what the processor provides: at 4.5 V for a 5-volt signal, at 2.5 V for a 3.3-volt one. On-resistance in the hundredths of an ohm, current rating with several times the margin, drain-source voltage with margin above the spikes, automotive grade AEC-Q101, as in the lesson on board components.
A gate resistor of around 100–220 Ω: it limits the gate charging current and damps ringing on the edges.
A gate-source resistor of around 10–100 kΩ: it holds the transistor off while the processor isn’t driving the input — otherwise the load could switch on from noise pickup.

Spike protection. When a coil — relay, valve, injector — turns off, an inductive spike appears at the drain, as in the lesson on the oscilloscope. In the chip, built-in protection absorbed it; a separate transistor has none. Fit a TVS diode (suppressor) or a Zener diode between drain and source, cathode to the drain; for a relay, a flyback diode to positive, across the coil, will also do.

An emulation resistor, if needed. The old chip left on the board may see the disconnected output as an open and set an “open circuit” code. A resistor from its lifted output to the positive feed from the main relay sometimes helps. The value comes from the datasheet, usually kilohms: the resistor barely warms up, and when the car is parked, with the relay off, no current flows through it.
A pulse from the processor turns the transistor on, and the TVS absorbs the spike at turn-off.

Diode or Zener: what’s the difference

A flyback diode to positive circulates the coil current back through the winding: there’s almost no spike, but the current decays slowly. A relay releases a moment later — no harm for it. An injector can’t work like that: while the current decays it is still open and delivers extra fuel, and the module calculates fuel delivery from the opening time. A Zener or TVS lets the spike rise only up to its own voltage, and the current decays quickly — as with the chip’s original protection. Choose a clamp voltage close to the one given in the burnt-out chip’s datasheet: it must be above any voltage the vehicle electrical system can have, otherwise the TVS will conduct all the time and overheat, and below the transistor’s maximum voltage.
With a diode, the current decays slowly; with a Zener or TVS, quickly.

The diode goes from the drain to the same positive that feeds the winding — then it effectively sits across the winding. If it’s a different positive, the module will be back-fed through the winding and the diode when it should be asleep. That’s why on the board it’s simpler to fit a TVS between drain and source: it suits any load.
Fitting it on the board

Make a memory backup, as in the lesson on module memory, and fix the cause that burnt out the channel, as in the lesson on output stages. A separate transistor has no built-in protection against shorts and overheating: if the cause isn’t fixed, it will burn out at the very first short.

Isolate the burnt-out channel: desolder and lift that channel’s output pin on the chip, or cut the trace from it to the connector. If the whole chip is shorted and loading the supply, it is removed — but only when all of its channels can be replaced the same way.

Take the signal from the burnt-out channel’s IN input or from the resistor through which the processor drives it. Check on a running module with an oscilloscope: pulses are present, amplitude 5 or 3.3 V. Use a neighboring working channel of the same chip and the datasheet to make sure a high level at the input switches the load on.

Drain — with wire no thinner than the trace — to the trace leading to the connector pin where the channel output was. Source — short and thick to power ground next to the driver’s ground pins, not to the signal ground near the processor.

Assemble the parts on a small board or right on the pads, and secure them together with the wires with glue against vibration, as in the lesson on moisture and vibration. The heat-sink tab of a power package is the drain: onto the module’s heat sink only through an insulating pad. With a relay or an injector, a transistor with low on-resistance barely warms up.
Conformal coating only after testing on the bench and in the car.

On the bench — with the factory load or a simulator: a lamp drawing no more current than the factory load, a real injector or relay. Get pulses with an actuator test from the scan tool or with a crank simulator.

Oscilloscope on the drain: off — supply voltage, on — almost zero, at turn-off — a spike cut off by a flat “plateau” at the TVS voltage. Compare with the neighboring original channels, as in the lesson on output stages: the shape should be similar.
After a few minutes of running, the transistor and the TVS should be barely warm.
Scan tool: no codes for this channel. “Open circuit” with a good load means you need an emulation resistor.
Then in the car: starting, codes in all modules, live data and a test drive, as in the lesson on handing over to the customer.

A code of 2–3 digits: each digit — a series of flashes, with a pause between digits. Each code is repeated 3 times, then the next one, in ascending order of numbers.

A two-digit code: the first series of flashes — the first digit, pause, the second series — the second digit (for example, 1 flash, pause, 4 flashes = “1,4”). Only one error is shown — the most important one.

A two-digit code: the first digit — 1–8 flashes, a pause of 1,5 s, the second digit — 1–6 flashes, then a pause of 4 s and the next code. The first digit — what is faulty (2 modulator, 3 sensor gap, 4 sensor open/short circuit, 5 unstable signal/tyre size, 6 toothed rotor, 7 system functions, 8 ABS unit). The second digit for codes 2–6 — the location: 1 right front, 2 left front, 3 right rear (drive axle), 4 left rear, 5 right of the additional axle, 6 left of the additional axle.
A two-digit code: first long flashes — the first digit, then short ones — the second. For example, 3 long and 2 short flashes = code 32.

A three-digit code: the first series of flashes — the first digit, a pause of about 1 s, the second series — the second digit, pause, the third series — the third digit. For example, 2 flashes — pause — 4 flashes — pause — 2 flashes = code 2-4-2. Codes are shown one per button press, after the last one the first one comes again.
A three-digit code: the first series of flashes — hundreds, after a pause — tens, after a pause — units. For example, 1 flash — pause — 2 flashes — pause — 4 flashes = code 1-2-4.

Idle speed hunts or the engine runs rough at idle
Idle speed hunts
Idle hunting: check for a vacuum leak

A common cause of a rough idle is a vacuum leak: extra air gets into the intake bypassing the mass air flow sensor (MAF) or downstream of the throttle — through a cracked intake hose, a vacuum line, the intake manifold gasket or the PCV valve. Signs: the idle hunts or jumps, the engine runs rough at idle, and lean codes P0171 and P0174 may set.

Carburetor cleaner is flammable. Spray in short, small bursts and only on cool parts of the intake — never on the exhaust manifold, ignition coils or plug wires. Keep a fire extinguisher nearby, don’t smoke, and don’t work in a closed garage.

Connect a scan tool and find intake manifold pressure (the MAP sensor). With the engine off and the ignition on it equals atmospheric pressure — about 900 mbar (90 kPa). The exact figure depends on where you are: the higher above sea level, the lower it is.

Start the engine and let it warm up. At idle intake pressure drops to roughly 300–400 mbar (30–40 kPa). Noticeably higher and wandering — suspect a vacuum leak; misfires or off timing can look the same.
Check the fuel trims: on a warm idle the sum of short- and long-term trim goes above +10…+15 % and drops at higher rpm — the typical picture of a vacuum leak.
A smoke machine finds the leak most precisely: smoke is fed into the intake and comes out wherever it isn’t sealed.

Without a smoke machine: with the engine running, lightly spray carburetor cleaner along the intake joints — from the MAF along the hose to the throttle body, along the intake manifold gasket and the vacuum lines. If the rpm rises for a moment, the leak is near that spot.
Check the obvious: clamps and the intake boot after the MAF, vacuum lines (cracks, popped-off hoses), the brake booster hose, the PCV valve, the oil filler cap and the dipstick.

I check for a vacuum leak with the scan tool first: with the engine off intake pressure is about 900 — that’s atmospheric; with it running, 300–400. If it’s higher at idle, I look for the leak with a smoke machine, and if I don’t have one handy I lightly spray carb cleaner along the intake from the MAF. If the rpm picks up, the leak is roughly there.
Oleg will smoke-test the intake, find the leak and fix it. Mobile service available.

Slipping: revs rise but the car doesn’t move

Gearbox slipping: revs rise but the car doesn’t move

The engine revs up but the car accelerates sluggishly or doesn’t move, and revs flare during shifts — that’s the gearbox slipping. It’s a fault in the gearbox itself: most often worn clutch packs inside or low fluid.
Don’t floor it to “get through”: slipping burns the clutches in minutes and makes the repair pricier. If it slips badly, call a tow truck.
Look under the car: a puddle of red or brown fluid means a gearbox leak — don’t drive on.
If the gearbox has a dipstick, check the fluid level and condition strictly per the manual (usually engine warm, lever in P). Dark fluid that smells burnt means burnt clutches.
See whether the gearbox light or Check Engine is on and decode the code in the “Error codes” tab. Slipping is usually logged as P0730–P0736 (incorrect gear ratio).
Fluid is fine but it still slips — internal wear: clutch packs, valve body. That’s a gearbox rebuild: go to automatic transmission specialists, not auto electricians.

If the engine revs but the car won’t go, it’s the gearbox hardware itself — the clutch packs. That’s not for electricians but for transmission shops that rebuild automatics. Before that you can check the fluid and read the codes so you arrive with a diagnosis.
Internal gearbox repair is done by automatic transmission specialists, not auto electricians. Oleg can read the gearbox codes with a scanner beforehand so you arrive with a ready diagnosis.
Kicks and jerks when shifting
Jolts when shifting or when selecting D and R come from a fault the gearbox control unit sees, from lost adaptations, or from the fluid: low, old or the wrong spec.
Run a diagnosis: read the gearbox codes with a scanner and decode them in the “Error codes” tab. Gearbox codes are usually P07xx.

No codes — one option is a gearbox adaptation: the learned values are reset with a scanner and the gearbox re-learns around the wear. Then drive calmly so it can “learn”; each gearbox has its own procedure.
Check the fluid: level, colour and smell, strictly per the manual. Low or old fluid also causes incorrect shifting. Use only fluid with the spec listed for your gearbox.
Check the battery and terminals: voltage dips make the gearbox control unit shift harshly.
If the kicks remain after adaptation and a fluid change, the gearbox needs repair at a transmission shop.
If the gearbox kicks, the first thing I do is a diagnosis. No codes — one option is an adaptation. And I always check the fluid: it can also cause incorrect shifting.
Oleg will run a scanner diagnosis of the gearbox and, if there are no codes, an adaptation. If the cause is inside the gearbox, he’ll tell you where to go.
The car goes forward but not in reverse, or the other way round. That means the fault is inside the gearbox itself: a worn or broken clutch pack, brake band or valve-body valve for that gear.
Don’t try to “force” the gear with throttle — you can finish the gearbox off.
Look at the dash: does the letter change to R (or D)? If not, first check the selector cable, as in “The lever moves but the car doesn’t go”.
If the gearbox has a dipstick, check the fluid level per the manual. A puddle of fluid under the car — don’t drive on.
Check the gearbox error code and decode it in the “Error codes” tab.
This is an internal gearbox repair: go to automatic transmission specialists, not auto electricians. Get there on a tow truck.
If the car only goes forward and not in reverse, or the other way round, the problem is in the gearbox itself. That’s a job for transmission shops that repair automatics, not electricians.
Repairs are done by automatic transmission specialists. Oleg can read the gearbox codes before the repair.

To get going I press the shift-lock release — it’s usually under a little cap near the selector. Then I check the fuses: the brake lights may be out. If the fuse is fine, I check the brake pedal switch.
First I check the brake-light fuse, then the brake pedal switch — it often breaks or falls out. To get going right now, use the shift-lock release under the cap by the selector.
Starter keeps cranking after start
Check Engine flashes, engine misfires
Starter keeps cranking after you release the key

You released the key (or the Start button) but the starter keeps cranking or whines with the engine running. This happens when the starter solenoid contacts stick, or when the starter’s thin wire keeps getting power — from the ignition switch, the starter relay or the wiring.
A starter that won’t disengage overheats in a minute or two, can melt the wiring and damage the flywheel ring gear. Shut the engine off at once and disconnect the battery’s negative terminal.
Turn the engine off and disconnect the battery’s negative terminal — the starter will stop.
Find the thin wire on the starter (the control wire on the solenoid) and disconnect it. Insulate its end so it can’t touch metal. Leave the thick power cable alone.

Reconnect the negative terminal. If the starter cranks again even with the thin wire off, the problem is the starter itself: the solenoid contacts are stuck. Disconnect the terminal again — the starter needs repair or replacing.

If the starter no longer cranks, the problem is the wiring: the thin wire is getting constant power. Check the starter relay (you can swap it with an identical relay in the box), the ignition switch contacts and the wire from the switch to the starter.
Don’t start the car until the cause is found: the starter may stay engaged again.
If the starter keeps cranking after the ignition key is released, I disconnect the thin wire from the starter. Still cranking — it’s the starter. Stopped — it’s the wiring, and I trace the circuit.
Oleg will find where the starter’s power comes from — relay, ignition switch or wiring — or remove the starter for repair. Call-outs available.
Flashing Check Engine: misfires

If Check Engine flashes erratically at start-up or while driving and the engine runs rough, those are misfires: the mixture isn’t igniting in a cylinder. The usual culprits are spark plugs, plug boots or ignition coils.
While the light flashes, go easy on the throttle and don’t drive far: unburnt fuel gets into the exhaust and can ruin the catalytic converter quickly.
Read the error code: P0300 means random misfires, P0301–P0308 a specific cylinder (the last digit is the cylinder number). Decode it in the “Error codes” tab.
Turn the engine off and inspect the coils and boots: cracks, arcing marks (white or dark tracks), oil in the plug wells, corroded connectors.
Remove the plugs: black soot, oil, a cracked insulator, a wide gap or a worn electrode — replace the plugs as a set.
Coil test: swap the coil from the misfiring cylinder with a neighbouring one. If the misfire “moves” to the other cylinder, the coil is bad. If it stays put, check the plug, injector and compression.
If misfires began after rain or an engine wash, dry out the plug wells and boots.

If Check Engine starts flashing erratically when the engine starts, it’s mostly misfires: plugs, boots or coils. I start with the error code — it points to the cylinder — then check the plug and swap the coils.
Oleg will read the codes, find the misfiring cylinder and check the plugs, boots and coils. Call-outs available.

Switch on the ignition (no need to start the engine) and choose your make or protocol in the scanner. Cheap ELM327 adapters don’t support every protocol and module.
Check power: between pins 16 and 4 (or 5) there should be 12–14 V, 24–28 V on a truck. No voltage — most often the cigarette lighter or OBD socket fuse has blown: they’re often shared.
Check ground: resistance between pins 4, 5 and the body should be about 0 Ω.

CAN bus: switch off the ignition and measure resistance between pins 6 and 14. Normal is about 60 Ω: two 120 Ω resistors at the bus ends. 120 Ω — one branch is open or a resistor is missing; about 0 — a short; infinite — an open circuit.
With the ignition on, pin 6 (CAN High) usually reads about 2.5–3.5 V and pin 14 (CAN Low) about 1.5–2.5 V to ground.
K-line (pin 7): about 12 V at rest. Zero or a constant 5 V means a module or the alarm is pulling the line down.
Power and bus are fine but still no communication — disconnect the alarm, GPS tracker and other devices on the OBD or CAN. A faulty module can also bring the bus down: unplug modules one at a time.

ABS
The anti-lock system is off. The brakes work, but the wheels may lock under hard braking.
Brake early and gently, especially on slippery roads.

Stability control (ESP)
Flashing on a slippery road means the system is working — that’s normal. Steady means it’s off or faulty.

The number stamped on the body matches the registration, with no signs of re-stamping
The stamping is usually on the engine bay bulkhead, under the mat by the front seat or on a pillar. Uneven digits, welding, filler or fresh paint around it — walk away.
The VIN read by the scanner from the control unit matches the registration
The scanner reads the VIN stored in the engine control unit (mode 09 in OBD). A different VIN or none means the unit was replaced: ask the seller why.

On a flat, straight road the car keeps going straight when you lightly let go of the wheel — no pull to either side

Find a flat, straight stretch with no ruts or slope and no traffic nearby. First make sure the tire pressures are equal. At 40–60 km/h, lightly let go of the wheel for a couple of seconds, keeping your hands close. The car should track straight and the wheel should stay centered. If it pulls left or right, the body geometry may be off after a crash or the wheel alignment may be out: have it checked on an alignment rack.
The mileage matches the engine hours (mostly on trucks and heavy equipment)

Engine hours are stored in the engine ECU, and they are usually not reset when the odometer is rolled back. Scan tools mostly show them on trucks and heavy equipment; few cars have this: no engine hours — skip this item. Approximate mileage = engine hours × average speed. For example, 10,000 engine hours on a long-haul tractor is roughly 400,000–600,000 km. Much less on the odometer — the mileage has most likely been rolled back.
The starter cranks, but the dash stays dark and the fuses are fine. The culprit was the ignition switch contact group — after replacing it, the car started.
Check Engine on: P0328 (knock sensor) and P0350 (coil circuit). The codes showed where to look — coils, plugs, wiring and the sensor — not what to replace right away.
The engine runs rough, code 31 — mass airflow sensor circuit. We checked the sensor connector and power; after the airflow sensor was replaced, Check Engine went out on its own.
Jerks while driving, Check Engine comes and goes: codes 19 and 14. An intermittent fault is caught by re-scanning when the jerks happen — no parts were swapped blindly.
The starter won’t crank, yet the interior lights don’t dim. The battery dropped to 9 V — we jump-started it. Bright lights don’t mean the battery is good.
Check Engine: P0421 and P0431 — the catalytic converters. The owner suspected the oxygen sensors, but these codes don’t confirm a sensor fault: the converters and exhaust are checked first.
ABS light on, turn signals, hazards and brake lights dead, the scan tool can’t see the ABS module (U0121). One of the ABS power wires had no voltage — with power supplied, the module came online.
Won’t start, P0343 and P0336 stored. After clearing, the codes didn’t come back. The fuel pump was getting power but not running — the pump and filter were replaced.
The battery was down to 3 V. After replacing it, we checked the parasitic draw — 10 mA, normal — and charging — 14.1 V under load. Only the old battery was to blame.
After suspension work, the ABS light comes on now and then: C1414 — front left wheel speed sensor. The sensor was removed and cleaned; an intermittent code is checked again when it shows up.

Won’t start and the key fob is dead: the fob battery was flat and the car battery was down to 2 V. We cleaned the terminals and jump-started it; after a discharge like that, the battery is best replaced before winter.
Won’t start, code P1200 — fuel pump circuit. The pump gets power, but it only ran after a light tap on the module cover — the pump needs replacing.
After throttle body cleaning, the idle stays around 1500 rpm. No codes, no vacuum leak — a throttle adaptation and idle relearn fixed it.
The 4WD light blinks, the instrument lights are off, 3 of 4 parking sensors don’t work. The instrument lights had simply been turned down with the dimmer.
The right turn signal flashes once and goes out; replacing the relay didn’t help. Wires left from a removed alarm were shorting to the body over bumps.
The engine ECU was faulty. A unit with the same part numbers was matched and paired to the factory immobilizer with a scan tool — about 35 minutes, and the car started.
The right turn signal stays on all the time; the hazard switch makes no difference. Unplugging the alarm connectors under the dash brought the turn signal back to normal.
Misfiring and stalling; the owner had already replaced the idle air control valve. Carb cleaner near the intake manifold smoothed the idle — a vacuum leak.
Won’t start, no sound from the fuel pump. The fuse and relay are fine, power reaches the pump module — the positive terminal on the module itself had burned.
Turn signals: bulb, relay or alarm

A turn signal flashing fast usually means a blown bulb on that side. Nothing flashes, not even the hazards — the fuse or flasher relay. One side stays on or flashes once and goes out — often an installed or removed alarm is to blame: its module and wires are tied into the turn signal circuits.

Don’t rush to replace the flasher relay blindly. On a Lexus ES300 the relay had already been replaced, but wires from a removed alarm were to blame. On a Toyota Highlander the right turn signal stayed on — unplugging the alarm connectors fixed it.
Oleg will find where the turn signal circuit drops out or shorts and properly disconnect leftover alarm wiring. Mobile service available.
Switch on the hazards. All turn signals flash — the relay and power are fine: look on the side that doesn’t work — bulb, connector, turn signal stalk.
One side flashes fast — a bulb has blown at the front, rear or in the side repeater on the fender. LED bulbs fitted without a load resistor flash the same way.

Nothing flashes, not even the hazards — check the turn signal and hazard fuse (below) and the flasher relay. On many newer cars the turn signals are run by the body control module — then a scan tool diagnosis is needed.

One side stays on and the hazards don’t change it, or the signal flashes once and goes out — check the alarm. Its module is usually under the dash in the driver’s footwell. Unplug its connectors: if the turn signal works normally, the problem is the alarm or how it was wired in.
If an alarm was removed earlier, look for leftover wires: over bumps they touch the body and short the turn signal circuit to ground.
Trailer turn signals don’t flash — check the trailer socket and its contacts: corrosion is a common cause.
Truck: trailer turn signals don’t flash — check the trailer socket and its contacts: corrosion is a common cause.
Instrument lights off: check the dimmer

Most often the illumination has simply been turned all the way down with the dimmer — a thumbwheel or buttons on the dash, or a setting in the instrument cluster menu. The instrument lights are also usually powered together with the parking lights: if the parking lights are off too, their fuse is to blame.
A Mitsubishi Pajero 2007 came in with the instrument lights off. The dimmer was in the wrong position — we turned it up and the lights came on. No bulbs or cluster repair were needed.
Turn on the parking lights or low beams and turn the dimmer all the way up. It can be a thumbwheel left of the steering wheel, buttons on the cluster or an item in the menu.
On many cars with automatic headlights the illumination is deliberately dimmed in daylight. Check in the dark or with the light sensor on the dash covered.
Parking lights are off too — check the parking light fuse (below): the instrument and switch illumination is often on the same fuse.
Parking lights work, the dimmer is at maximum, but there’s no illumination — the dimmer, the cluster connector or the cluster itself needs checking.
If the idle went high or started hunting right after cleaning the throttle body, run a throttle adaptation and idle relearn with a scan tool: the ECU remembers the corrections for the dirty throttle.

Stage 1: the DEF light is on — low level. Stage 2: DEF + Check Engine — even lower level, wrong DEF or SCR fault, slight power loss. Stage 3: DEF almost empty, wrong DEF or an SCR fault lasting over 5 hours — the DEF light flashes, major power loss. Stage 4: + red Stop Engine after refuelling without adding DEF, an hour of idling or a stop — speed limited to 5 mph (~8 km/h); since 2026 Cummins has been releasing US software updates with a final stage of 25 mph. What to do: fill DEF to ISO 22241; if the lights stay on, go to Oleg straight away.

Below 10% — yellow segment and alert; below 5% — red segment, buzzer once per second and engine torque limitation; empty tank — power and engine speed limitation, the machine must be moved to a safe place and filled with AdBlue. If the SCR system fails — three steps: message, power limitation, then power and engine speed limitation; contact Oleg.

Check the glow plug: connect it to the control unit and start — a good one glows from the tip towards the middle. If it glows from the middle or down to the base — replace it. If a good glow plug glows weakly — the control unit is faulty (contact Oleg).
A screen not seated all the way causes start failures. No mandrel — better contact Oleg.
Do not spill fuel; wipe up drips immediately. If the heater fails to start twice in a row with the line full — contact Oleg.
If the pump still does not work — it is replaced as a whole unit; its output is checked with a UPT-4 device — contact Oleg.

Contact Oleg: the heater must be removed, the blower, adapter, combustion chamber and heat exchanger disassembled and damaged gaskets replaced, and after the repair the manual requires testing the heater on a test bench — at maximum, exhaust no hotter than 500 °C and carbon monoxide (CO) no more than 0.1 %. A leaking heat exchanger must not be used. The manufacturer recommends a check at least once a year.

Clear the hot-air inlet and outlet and contact Oleg: according to the manual, the lockout is cleared only with diagnostics, because an overheat that has happened three times needs checking. A normal (non-locking) error is reset by pressing any button on the remote; switch on again — no sooner than 5–10 s later. The manufacturer advises eliminating the cause of overheating immediately after the first occurrence.
A loosely seated screen causes start failure. The manual does not specify a press-fitting tool — if in doubt, contact Oleg.

Three errors 13 in a row lock the heater (code 37) — if it still has not ignited after a couple of retries, find the cause or go to Oleg.
